queen mary's veterans hospital, Montreal

1.	At Queen Mary's veterans hospital, Montreal, how are the doctors appointed?
2.	What research is being done at Queen Mary's veterans hospital, particularly with reference to heart and blood vessels?
3.	What facilities are present at Queen Mary's veterans hospital for the treatment of paraplegics?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
1.	There are, at present, employed at Queen Mary's veterans hospital 13 full-time doctors and 130 part-time doctors. Full-time doctors are employed through the civil service commission by the usual procedure.
The part-time doctors are appointed pursuant to a recommendation by the medical advisory board of Queen Mary's, consisting of the chiefs of the various services. A large percentage of these part-time doctors are also on the faculties of medicine of McGill and, in those cases, the recommendation of the university is obtained. The recommendation, if concurred in by the director general 50433-3421
of treatment services, Department of Veterans Affairs, is submitted to the minister for approval.
By this method of employing part-time specialists and consultants, largely connected with universities, it is possible to employ highly skilled doctors.
2.	Because the average age of veteran patients in Queen Mary's veterans hospital is above that found in civilian hospitals and because the department has clinical records for many years, this group of patients is ideal for the study of diseases of the heart and blood vessels which occur most frequently in older people.
At Queen Mary's studies are being undertaken to determine the effect of various diets on diseases of the blood vessels which in turn may cause strokes or coronary thromboses. The effects of certain drugs are also being studied in the hope of finding some method of preventing the onset and progress of these vessel diseases.
In the department of physics at McGill University, the Department of Veterans Affairs has set up a special ultracentrifuge which examines the blood of patients having blood vessels diseases. By its use it is hoped that early indications of vessel diseases may be detected and progression prevented.
3.	There is at Queen Mary's a very modem wing of 30 beds specially equipped to treat paraplegics. The treatment is carried out with the most modern equipment and using the facilities of the department of physical medicine at the hospital.
These 30 beds are continuously occupied and there are about 150 admissions a year of which 30 are new admissions. Where there are vacancies, treatment is made available to civilian patients.
The tremendous advance in the treatment of paraplegics is illustrated by the results of treatment at Queen Mary's. Of 75 new cases admitted between 1945 and 1955, only 2 have died, 5 remain in institutions, and the other 68 have been successfully rehabilitated. Before world war II, 85 per cent of all paraplegics died in the first three months after their accidents.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few general remarks on this measure, which obviously is one of the most important to come before the house because from it we realize considerably more than half our revenue, if my calculations are correct. The total receipts for the first two months are approximately $600 million, of which $375 million comes from income tax. At the time of his budget speech the minister is at great pains to predict as accurately as he can the receipts and disbursements over the year. We now have the chance of doing a partial stocktaking, two months' stocktaking, because we have the minister's statement covering the first two months.
I believe it is relevant to do this stocktaking because, in theory at least, it might be possible that the result of the two months might have been so much better or so much worse than the minister's estimates that he might come to us at this time with suggestions that he was going to make proposals different from what he made two months ago. Therefore I propose to read this brief statement which sets out the most important figures, and then to ask the minister certain questions based on this statement, all pursuant to what I suggest is the useful exercise of a two months' stocktaking. The statement is a press release of June 25, and I read part of it which gives us the figures:
Budgetary revenues for May were $382-3 million or $7-8 million less than for May last year, while expenditures were $278-2 million or $32-6 million more than a year ago. The budgetary surplus for May was $104-1 million compared with $144-5 million for May 1954.
For the first two months of the current fiscal year budgetary revenues were $611-3 million, expenditures were $474-7 million and the surplus was $136-6 million. For the first two months of 1954-55 revenues were $635-6 million, expenditures were $461-4 million and the budgetary surplus was $174-2 million.
I hope, when the minister comes to speak, he will himself comment on these figures, going into considerable detail and telling us where the results are better and where they are worse than he anticipated two months ago; in other words, putting us as far as possible in a position to look at the situation with his own eyes and with the knowledge that he has. Now I wish to draw his attention to certain figures in the statement and ask him if he will comment on them particularly.
I now read from the summary of budgetary revenues and expenditures. First of all, I would draw to his attention the fact that for the month of May the personal income tax figures are rather surprisingly down from

those of May a year ago. I would ask him to comment on that fact. I then go on to ask him to comment on certain other things, such as for example, the fact that the national defence expenditures are substantially up, as was the case in April also. I go on to draw his attention to the post office, public works and transport, on all of which I should like him to comment. Then I come to certain non-budgetary transactions such as the S15 million in the exchange fund account and the $25 million in the securities investment account.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I interrupt the hon. gentleman just to ask him whether he considers it would be relevant to this debate on income tax to comment upon the increased expenditures in certain departments?

I submit, Mr. Speaker- as I have tried to suggest-that we now have the opportunity, with two months' evidence before us, to ask the minister to comment on his forecast. Surely he will be able to do that because he will know the figures he had in mind. He will know the departments which have done better than he expected and those which have done worse and I suggest he will be able to enable us to discharge our duty which is, after all, to know all that we can about the finances of our country. With two months' evidence before him he will be able to do what I call stocktaking and to put us in the position that he now is in, whereby we will be better able to judge the likely results of the year. Mr. Speaker, I suggest that that stocktaking is all the more important in a year in which our budget will show a deficit. Indeed, I cannot imagine anything which is more relevant to the consideration of the bill which is going to bring in something over $2 billion of revenue and one which, incidentally, provides for certain reductions which we all welcome. As I said, it is conceivable-although we know it is not an actual fact-that the situation might have altered to the point that the minister was going to propose certain alterations in the recommendations of two months ago.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, with deference I suggest that there is nothing more relevant in considering a bill, the principle of which is to raise $2 billion, than for us to know just whether the minister has any fresh evidence or whether there are any new situations which confront him, in order to enable us to judge the situation upon which we are called upon to take action in this measure, as I say, for the raising of $2 billion. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak for
only a moment. This bill is introduced for the purpose of amending the Income Tax Act. I deeply regret that the minister has not yet seen fit to include in the bill a provision to remove the 3 per cent floor in relation to the deductibility of medical expenses, for income tax purposes. I hope the next time he brings in a bill of this kind he will include such an amendment, for it is long overdue.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the exchange that has taken place between Your Honour and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) as to what constitutes the principle of the bill before us. Perhaps after

Income Tax Act
listening to the discussion, and to the hon. member's suggestion that Your Honour should define the principle, I may be overbold in suggesting that it appears to me that at least three principles are involved in this bill to amend the Income Tax Act.
The first of these is as to whether or not this amending bill makes the necessary provision for the raising of funds through this medium. The second is as to what the impact on the economy of the country may be as a result of the changes proposed in the bill now before us.
So far as I am concerned, I feel those principles have been fairly thoroughly discussed in the budget debate, the debates on unemployment, and in other debates; and I do not propose to enter into any discussion of those aspects of the bill. However, I think there is another important principle involved in this bill to amend the Income Tax Act, and that is as to whether or not it removes any existing inequities in the application of the income tax which heretofore may have existed.
My contention is that this bill does not remove those inequities as it should, and I have one example I should like to mention in this debate on second reading of the bill. I have gone through its provisions and have tried to digest them. I have found that the reading of the provisions in resolution form is somewhat simpler and, having read them, it does appear to me that the amendments being proposed, speaking generally, seem to concern themselves much more with changes in the income tax as they affect, for example, people who are going to be issuing capital stock, and the expenses involved in connection with shares, than in removing some of the existing inequities in the Income Tax Act as they apply to ordinary taxpayers whose incomes are derived from wages or salaries.
I am not in agreement with the proposal of an across-the-board percentage of decrease in the application of the personal income tax, but at the moment I shall not enlarge upon that point. I should like however to refer briefly to a question I raised last year in connection with income tax, one concerning which I have had correspondence with the minister. I refer to deductions of expenses involved in the earning of a living by people whose incomes are derived almost entirely from wages and salaries. I feel that people whose incomes come from other sources are in a more favoured position in the matter of making deductions for expenses from taxable income than are people who receive their incomes from wages and salaries. To my mind this bill does not meet the situation satisfactorily.

As a specific example I would refer once again to the plight faced by large bodies of workers who, in the course of earning their living, of necessity must travel long distances from their normal places of residence and must incur the added expenses of board and lodging while away from home. They also incur certain other expenses in connection with the earning of their living.
I have in my hand a copy of a brief submitted to the minister on behalf of the loggers in the coastal areas of British Columbia, and which the minister has assured me would receive consideration. Apparently, however, it has not received sufficient consideration. In my opinion expense payments necessarily incurred in the earning of their living should be deductible for income tax purposes, for that group of workers, just as they are for other groups within the country. This group specifically suggested that some allowance should be made with respect to the cost of transportation to and from their place of employment in the remote areas. Some consideration should be given to the man who is faced with the problem of maintaining a home in a city and at the same time having to pay additional board and lodging while he is absent from his home. To my way of thinking, these are practical suggestions and ones which could very easily have been included in the present bill.
The third suggestion they make is with respect to certain special articles of clothing which that particular group of workers is required to have as a condition of being able to earn their living, such things, for example, as special caulk boots and hard hats. Last year when I raised this question I pointed out that all of the items I have referred to would be deductible for income tax purposes if the expenses were paid out by the employers of those people. They would then be deducted as business expenses. I submit, Mr. Speaker, it is not an equitable state of affairs when the employer is permitted to deduct such things as an expense item in the cost of doing business, and the man who is dependent entirely upon a wage or a salary, and whose income tax is very easily deductible at source, is not given the same privilege.
If one examines the forms on which income tax returns must be made he finds that the T-l short form, which is used by people whose incomes come from wages and salaries, is a form which by its very nature precludes the opportunity for any sort of deduction of that kind at all; whereas the people who use the T-l general form certainly have some opportunities within that form of claiming exemptions for certain expenses. Included among those who use the T-l general are the

farmers and the fishermen of this country. Provision is made for those groups, as I pointed out last year also, to deduct, for example, a certain amount for small tool expenses. There again is an example of how, because of the circumstances under which the income is derived, large groups of people have an opportunity to claim exemptions which are denied to groups of tradesmen in the country, who, as a condition of being able to carry on their employment, must necessarily incur quite substantial expenses for small hand tools. And yet, under the present act and under the proposed amending bill, if it becomes law, they will still be denied any medium through which they can receive the equivalent deductions.
There is one other matter which I feel could very well have been provided for in this amendment to the Income Tax Act. That has to do with the problem faced by many of the young people of this country who are attempting to finance their way through university. As I understand it, if a parent has the kind of income which will enable him to provide education for his children, and the kind of income which will enable him to support them during the vacation period in the summertime when they are not in school, in other words, if he can claim them as being wholly dependent children, then he is in a position to receive certain exemptions on his taxable income on that account. On the other hand, a man who is not in that position and whose sons or daughters go out during the vacation period and work at gainful employment, and are not wholly dependent upon him, loses the right to claim them as wholly dependent children when they are engaged in acquiring a higher education. At the same time, the young people who are working are liable for income tax if their income reaches a figure above the basic exemption.
This is an instance where the bill does not remove an existing inequity from the income tax structure. There are other instances, but I do not want to prolong the debate on this subject. I do feel that the bill before the house is not one which carries out the principle which I have suggested, namely, removing a number of inequities from the income tax structure.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations on the second reading of this bill. I suppose that of all the bills that come before parliament in any session the bill to amend the Income Tax Act is without doubt the most complicated in its provisions. It seems to me that for that reason there could be
Income Tax Act
some improvement in the way in which we handle these bills. I recall that-I think it was two years ago-the Minister of Finance arranged with those members of the opposition who were particularly interested in tax questions to sit down with his senior officials and draftsmen and have an informal discussion together. That was a helpful procedure because no Minister of Finance, no matter how clear may be his own understanding of the provisions, or how lucid his attempted explanations in the house, can, it seems to me, clarify the intent and effect of the provisions of so technical a bill as well as can be done in an informal discussion of the sort that was used a couple of years ago.
I suggest that in aid of better understanding of these technical bills and also in aid of expediting the consideration of them in the house.
Sir, the bill before us is no exception to the normal routine followed in respect of the annual bill to amend the Income Tax Act. It represents a sifting out by the Minister of Finance of what are undoubtedly many proposals that come to him for changes in the act. No doubt most of the proposals that have come to him from sources outside government circles are proposals seeking some modification in the provisions of the act, either in the rates or in those provisions having to do with the exemption of income from the application of some of the taxing provisions, or applying exempting provisions of the act to certain individual cases or groups of cases. From government circles no doubt the minister receives proposals of a different nature, proposals arising directly from the administration, where difficulties or injustices may arise which were not contemplated when the provisions in question were enacted previously by the house. And then there is always the question of rates as well. From all these the minister makes his selections and brings them before the house in the form of a bill.
There are many individual amendments to the act in this bill. The minister has not been idle in dealing with the proposals which have come before him. Obviously this bill represents a sifting out or a winnowing of the proposals that have come before him, and the house is now being asked to give effect to this selection.
We may agree with many of them. So far as they are remedial, I am sure the house will agree, but I should like to make one observation. These are the results of the winnowing out of a multitude of proposals which come before the minister, particularly in the months immediately preceding the preparation and the introduction of the budget. They are not winnowings out that are carried on by parliament in any sense. Unquestionably when

Income Tax Act
many groups make representations to the minister they are under the impression, an erroneous one, that they are being made to parliament or to members of parliament. Some groups which are more experienced in these matters do take the precaution when submitting briefs to the minister and discussing them with him and his senior officials of sending copies of the brief to members of parliament. Others do not always realize that that is the way in which members of parliament come to know, apart from individuals or representatives of organizations speaking to them directly, what alterations are considered necessary in the Income Tax Act.
I realize that in this respect government policy is involved. None of these proposals can be put before the house in amendment or legislative form unless the government is prepared under our constitutional practice to sponsor them. I realize also that the minister is in frequent contact with interested bodies. There are certain groups in this country who are particularly engaged in a constant study of tax problems, whether in the larger field of rates and the form and nature of taxation or within the more minute range of problems arising out of administration.
The bill before us contains some decreases, but let it not be forgotten that there are also some increases in tax rates. The bill contains some new inclusions and some exclusions from income. The most spectacular change is the 2 per cent reduction in the rates of personal and corporation taxes. When I say 2 per cent I refer to the reduction of two points in the tax percentage.
There is one aspect of the reduction in the rate of corporation tax which should not escape the attention of the house at this time. I do not say that it was not mentioned in the budget debate, but it is certainly something which the house should have before it in approaching this bill. Section 39 of the Income Tax Act divides corporations into two classes. First of all it takes those with taxable incomes not exceeding $20,000, those in what we could term the small corporation class, and then there are the larger corporations with taxable incomes exceeding $20,000 per year. The rates in effect on those two classes of corporation have been respectively 20 per cent in the case of the small corporation, and 49 per cent in the case of the larger corporation if you include the two percentage points which are added on account of contributions to the old age security fund. I am riot overlooking the fact that in the calculation of the tax payable by corporations with incomes over $2b,000 they pay the lower rate on the first $20,000 of their income.

I hope it has not escaped the attention of hon. members of this house that the reduction which the minister has proposed and which this bill now will bring into effect in the corporation tax rate is a reduction confined to the second class of corporation. It does not extend to the first class of corporation. There is no reduction in the rate applicable to those corporations whose taxable income does not exceed $20,000. In my submission that is a regrettable exclusion. It is a regrettable oversight; no doubt an intentional oversight, and therefore the more regrettable. That reduction is denied to small companies or to companies in receipt of the smaller taxable income.
When these remedial provisions in favour of corporations with a taxable income of not over $20,000 were introduced several years ago by the then minister of finance they were generally hailed by all parts of the house as being sound fiscal legislation. Here was an opportunity that was being grasped to encourage the growth of business. Here was encouragement being given to the flowering of free enterprise in order that men in this country might be encouraged to start up in business in a small way, to exercise their skill, ingenuity, resourcefulness and hard work in order to start businesses. We understood the principle to be encouragement for the general good of the establishment of as many businesses as could survive the economic tests of the times. If that principle was sound, and it was conceived to be sound by all parties in this house, what principle now justifies the minister in confining the reduction in the corporation tax to those corporations whose taxable income exceeds $20,000 per annum? It seems to me that we are taking a retrograde step.
The minister will say that these young corporations, many of them small corporations, have since had an opportunity to grow. Surely the birth of small corporations is not a process that is to stop. Surely this process within the constant operation of our economic system and the economic growth of this country is continuous, and the kind of encouragement that was thought to be sound and wise four or five years ago for the benefit of small companies surely is just as sound and wise and as necessary today.
Actually today we have a much higher proportion of our population unemployed than was the case when this legislation was first introduced to give special tax and fiscal benefits to the small corporation. I should have thought that there would be strong reasons today for at least dealing with all corporations alike, but if there is to be any

discrimination as between corporations with small incomes and those with large incomes there should certainly not be discrimination against the small corporations. Yet that is what this legislation does. It effects a reduction in the total income tax levied on the corporations with incomes over $20,000 to 47 per cent. But it leaves the rate static at 20 per cent on the corporations whose incomes do not exceed $20,000 or on the first $20,000 for corporations whose taxable incomes exceed $20,000.
There is one other aspect to this matter where in my submission the minister has failed to take advantage of an opportunity to give some sound fiscal assistance to small businesses. This ceiling on income was set at $20,000 about five years ago. At that time $20,000 meant more in purchasing power than $20,000 means today. It seems to me that the time has come for an upward revision in this ceiling that is now put upon the permissible income of these corporations that enjoy the benefit of the lower rate. Therefore, as earnestly as I can, I urge that if it is not too late the minister should reconsider his refusal to share with small corporations the benefit of the reductions that he is offering to corporations with incomes of $20,000 or over. At the same time he should give the most serious consideration to raising that $20,000 ceiling, which in my submission is no longer an adequate or fair test to apply as between the two classes of corporations.
I hope that no words I have uttered will be regarded as indicating any antipathy toward or disapproval of the proposed reduction in the rate of taxation applied to the larger corporations. We hear from some in this house from time to time claiming that there should not be reductions in the rate of corporation income tax, and we even hear demands that the rate of corporation income tax ought to be increased.

Income Tax Act
However, there are many things in our income tax legislation that need to be reviewed. The Minister of Finance has now been in office for 364 days. Tomorrow, I believe, marks the first anniversary of his having been sworn in to his present office. I can assure him that the good will that I expressed to him at that time on taking up the heavy burden and heavy responsibility that he carries goes to him still in the fullest measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Thank you.

I am sure that the experiences he has had this year in facing, no doubt, a multitude of deputations and wrestling with a multitude of problems-perhaps some of them not new to him, but no doubt many of them new

may have inclined him to view sympathetically the suggestion I should like to make to him, that there should be some form of periodical parliamentary review of this taxing legislation. I am thinking particularly of the Income Tax Act.
When the old income war tax act was supplanted by the present Income Tax Act some six or seven years ago, there was a general revision of the legislation. There was a reference of the bill to the banking and commerce committee. I believe that much more than that type of reference is required to achieve the purpose I have in mind. There we were not permitted to hear the observations of anyone outside the committee. The Minister of Finance indicated that government policy was represented in every section of the bill and therefore there could not be any amendments that did not conform with the constitutional usage.
It seems to me, without subtracting anything from the responsibility of the government or the special responsibility that rests upon the shoulders of the Minister of Finance in regard to the form and nature of amendments to our taxing legislation year by year, that it would be highly useful, not only to the government but also to parliament, to the taxpaying public and in particular to business, which faces the brunt of most of the difficult tax problems that arise, if there could be some form of public review whereby organizations which have made intensive study of our tax legislation and the problems that arise in the course of its administration would have an opportunity of putting their proposals before some wider forum than simply before the minister and his officials. I realize that any such proposals, if they are to be given effect, will still require to have the approval of the government. The minister and his officials sitting with him no doubt will still be required to give approval to them. But our tax legislation, and in particular our Income Tax Act, has now become fMr. Fleming.]
so complicated in its provisions that there are few people who can give an intelligent reading to that legislation. Arising from it there are many problems that require a public hearing in the presence of more than just the minister and his senior officials. It seems to me that having regard to these problems there should be given the opportunity of a periodic general review of the legislation and I hope, in consequence, a periodic general revision as required.
I just give you one example, Mr. Speaker, because I do not wish to prolong my remarks on second reading. I cite this problem just by way of example. It does not appear in the bill. It was not referred to in the minister's budget speech. However, it is the sort of problem that requires serious consideration. We have that provision to which I referred and the right on the part of the individual taxpayer to deduct from the tax he would otherwise pay 20 per cent of the dividends he has received from Canadian corporations which have already been subjected to Canadian income tax. There arises the relation of that form of deduction to the man whose wife is in receipt of an income largely made up of dividends of that nature and whose income is not of taxable amount. As things stand today it seems to me that there is a denial of the full intent of the 20 per cent deduction in a case of that kind. The matter was brought to the attention of the minister in the brief submitted to him by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, dated February 10, 1955. I shall read just one short paragraph from that brief. It refers to section 38 and section 26 (2) under the heading "Tax Credit on Dividends received by a Tax-exempt Spouse", and reads as follows:
When the income of a wife is over $250 but below $1,000, the excess of her income is in effect added to the income of her husband through a reduction of his marital exemption. If the income of the wife is composed of dividends, the 20 per cent tax credit is lost. Accordingly, it is recommended by the executive council that in such cases the husband be allowed the 20 per cent tax credit on that portion of the dividends received by his wife on which he has to pay tax.
In brief enlargement of that statement I point out this result, and it is one that has been in my mind for some time because I have seen the effect of it in preparing income tax returns for clients. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) will recall discussion related to this particular problem when he was parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance because that was in the days of the introduction of the 20 per cent deduction. Here is a case where, if the income of the spouse is from bond interest or other forms of investment income, apart from dividends, and

her income amounts to $700, that income so far as her husband is concerned is in exactly the same position as the income of another taxpayer whose wife has an income of $700 a year and that income is entirely composed of dividends from Canadian corporations which have already been subjected to Canadian corporation income tax. In that situation, the intended benefit of the 20 per cent deduction is entirely lost. Neither the husband nor the wife derives any benefit from it.
I have selected that point out of many that could be raised, simply as an example of the sort of thing that, it seems to me, requires a forum for discussion which this committee of ways and means, so large in numbers and under such pressure of time, does not adequately afford.

On clause 1 there is a point that I should like to raise with regard to section 11, subsection 1 (1) of the existing Income Tax Act. In regard to this section which I will outline in a moment, I would suggest that the interpretation of the regulations under the act have raised an inequity concerning certain orders made by certain courts. The section generally provides for deductions from personal income tax of certain payments and expenses and this particular subsection sets out the requirements regarding the payments for the maintenance of a wife or children of a marriage where there has been divorce, separation or anything of that nature. There are three requirements: An order for divorce or judicial separation-I may say we have no action for judicial separation in Ontario-a written separation agreement, or alimony payments on a periodic basis. If you come under any of these three and the parties are living apart, such payments can be deducted for income tax purposes.
In Ontario most of this type of work is done by what we call the family court. The family court is not recognized by the income tax officials as a court or at least as a competent judicial body; "a competent tribunal" are the words used in the section. Hence any payments made pursuant to an order of the family court in Ontario are not deductible. I would respectfully suggest that this situation results in some inequity with regard to the act. As I say, the family court handles the bulk of this sort of thing in Ontario.
Income Tax Act
Because of this fact and because of the special training the family court officials have received, I think they are highly competent to consider and to dispose of these domestic difficulties.
I can best put this point across by giving the committee a concrete example of how this thing works out. This is an actual case that occurred in Ontario recently. Mr. X and his wife separated about 10 years ago because of incompatibility and Mrs. X promptly made an application in the family court under the Deserted Wives' and Children's Maintenance Act. An order was made providing maintenance for her and separate amounts for their children. This order was varied on several occasions until it reached $50 per month for the wife and $35 per month for each of the three children. At no time would it have been possible because of the feeling between the parties to arrange a separation agreement between themselves. I might point out here that a separation agreement is merely made between the two parties and has no authority of a court behind it other than any other simple contract between two parties but payments made under a separation agreement are deductible. I will go on with the case. In 1952 in this case a writ for divorce was issued and served and the action was heard in the early part of 1954. The husband had continued to make payments through the family court regularly. When the action was heard the judge followed the award of the family court as far as the wife was concerned and increased it to $60. He stated however that he would not disturb the findings of the family court since he recognized their competence regarding the children. The net result is as follows: Mr. X will be paying the sum of $720 per year to his wife which will be deducted for income tax purposes. He will also be paying the sum of $1,260 per year for the support of his children which he may not be able to deduct. I think the situation as I have tried to set it out there is obvious. The income tax officials have ruled definitely that payments made by virtue of an order of the family court cannot be deducted. My suggestion is that this does provide an inequity and I would ask the minister to give some consideration to changing this situation. Perhaps we do not need any amendment. I do not think any amendment to the act would be necessary. It merely calls for some directive or some new attitude of mind on the part of those who are responsible for interpreting the words, "competent tribunal", as set out in section 11, subsection 1 (1).

The first point is that clause 1 is one of the remedial provisions of the bill, and therefore I am sure will be welcome so far as it goes. There are two questions that occur to me in regard to it. The first is as to why, if the legislation were sound, it could not have been given some retroactive effect, at least to recent times.
The subject matter of this section arises, as I think the minister will agree, out of litigation which was disposed of in the courts not so very long ago. Some taxpayers had to incur considerable expense and run the gamut of the courts in order to find at the end that, in addition to paying the tax on that portion of their income which had been expended for the purpose indicated in this section, they had to pay the costs as well.
Now, in a situation of that kind where the government recognizes after a case has run through the courts that the law ought to be changed to conform with the interpretation of the law which the taxpayer in the litigation sought to uphold, and where the government has then decided to sponsor legislation to change the law there is a strong case made out for making remedial legislation retroactive.
The rule, of course, is that we frown upon retroactive legislation where it imposes a burden in any form upon the subject. But that rule does not apply in the case of remedial legislation, as you well know, Mr. Chairman. It seems to me in a case of that kind, in all fairness, the government ought to give very serious consideration to making legislation of that kind retroactive. Now, I realize the difficulty where you are introducing retroactive legislation even of a remedial kind, of putting in an effective date. But in this particular situation, having regard to the history of litigation that is antecedent to this provision of the bill, it seems to me there was every reason for making the remedial legislation retroactive.
The second point I should like to make on the section relates to the extent of the expenses which the taxpayer is now permitted to deduct under section 11 of the act, thereby reducing his taxable income. The explanatory note to the section speaks of the paragraph providing "that the taxpayers may claim a deduction for certain expenses in the course of issuing shares or borrowing money." I have an amendment to move to clause 1. Perhaps I may read the explanation of it before I ask my colleague the Minister of National Revenue to move it.
Under section 11 (1) (h) of the Income Tax Act, which has been in the law for a number of years, an employer is allowed a deduction for a lump sum paid to fund a pension for a retiring employee. However, the present law allows this deduction only if the amount is paid in the year the employee retires or becomes eligible to retire. Certain of these plans now provide that the employee shall have a vested right to benefits under the plan after a certain number of years of employment, even if he does not remain with the employer until he reaches the age for retirement stipulated under the plan. If such an employee with vested rights terminates his employment before reaching retirement age the employer has to make a payment to provide the pension benefits, but under a strict interpretation of the present wording of the law this payment is not deductible either at the date of termination or later because at the time of termination the employee is not eligible to retire and when he does reach retirement age he is not an employee of the employer involved.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I have an amendment which I would ask my colleague the Minister of National Revenue to move, which carries out the purpose in changing the law as I have outlined, that is to provide for the employer a tax deduction on a lump sum payment he has made and which, by a strict interpretation that I referred to, is not deductible at the present time.

I had intended to ask a question before the amendment was moved, in which I was about to point out that I believe it is unusual to have negative expressions in a clause of this kind. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
From the time when these special advantages were given to those who would develop and derive earnings from mines, there has been no specific definition of such mines, except that contained in this section. At one time undoubtedly the purpose was to compensate, if that is the proper word, those who were developing the country and who were risking money for purposes of that development. In that connection certain types of concessions were granted. We had in mind always the risky ventures, ones in remote areas which would require at least the risk of considerable sums of money to bring them into production, rather than the more obvious items such as, for example, sand pits. These are on the surface, and it is easy to see whether they will yield a return, and that can be found out without very much difficulty if one is able to estimate accurately. I agree with the hon. member that it is unusual to have negative expressions in a bill. Nevertheless the purpose of these words is to define a mine, actually, and to define it from time to time as circumstances arise which would make it necessary to interpret the policy of exemption.
I agree with what the hon. member said earlier, that if one had a general revision of the bill there is no doubt this type of thing would receive a good deal of attention. I think he would agree with me however that changes in definition would have to take place as circumstances arose, and as requests were made for exemptions in respect of new projects. You would have to judge in each case whether it came within the terms of your stated policy.
Income Tax Act

I hope no difficulty will arise under the new definition. It would seem that the general intent of the section is to place on a permanent basis the exemptions which hitherto have been on a three-year basis. I am sure there will be general agreement with that purpose. However, the new form of definition is a quite wide departure from the form which has existed up to this time. The present section simply provides:
Where a corporation establishes that a mine was
(a)	a metalliferous mine, or
(b)	an industrial mineral mine certified by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to have been operating on mineral deposits (other than bedded deposits except sylvite).
This is a radical change in the form of definition. I think it will be appreciated by all hon. members that when a specific enumeration is employed, even where as in this instance it is an enumeration couched in terms of exclusion, difficulties may arise. I would express the hope that sufficient thought has been given to the new definition that no difficulties are likely to arise within the next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Difficulties may arise, of course; but at the moment none of the projects which are now redefined is receiving the advantage of this section.

I would ask the minister whether this clause, and subsequent clauses with regard to depreciation, implement exactly the items in the Income Tax Act. In other words the intention is to implement what is here, and not to go beyond that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.

In those circumstances I would like to put on record one or two comments regarding depreciation, because I wish to have them before the minister. I think also they should be on record.
The amendment, as I understand it, will permit oil or mining companies to expense expenditures on either oil or mining exploration in cases where the expenditures were incurred otherwise than on the company's own account, in consideration for shares or an option or right to purchase shares of a corporation on whose account the expenditures were incurred. This would have application where a company participates in the exploration of mining or oil properties with others, through the medium of a corporation set up specifically to hold those properties and to explore them.
This amendment does not apply to oil company mergers and amalgamations, of which there have been a number in recent years. There still does not appear to be any provision made or contemplated in the statutes whereby such mergers can be carried out without the successor company losing

Income Tax Act
the benefit of the expenditures for drilling and exploration costs to which its predecessor or predecessors would have been entitled.
This problem is a serious one, especially for shareholders of the smaller Canadian oil companies which have in recent years been merged with others, or which may have to be consolidated in the future in order to survive. Reasons for mergers are usually the conventional ones-economy in operations, reduction in overhead, consolidation of properties, provision of additional finances, the fight for survival. Practically all such companies have incurred expenditures for exploration in excess of their income in anticipation of the application of such expenditures against future taxable income. The right to charge off those accumulated losses against hoped-for future income is not extended, under present tax policy, to a successor company.
If for no other reason than that the policy discriminates against the thousands of small Canadian investors in smaller Canadian oil and mining companies, I trust that the government will not delay too much longer in amending the Income Tax Act to permit carrying over into company consolidations and mergers the right to write off qualified exploration expenditures. The Canadian Petroleum Association, I might say, has been urging such a step on the government for some 17 months.
Let's consider now depletion allowances, which as now constituted in Canada place the Canadian company at a competitive disadvantage with American companies in the acquisition of and development of Canadian oil and gas resources. While it is vitally important that we have a continued large inflow of foreign capital, particularly American investment, it is at least equally important that the maximum possible Canadian investment and equity be maintained in our own resources. Revision of present depletion allowance policy would go a long way toward increasing the Canadian stake in our western resources, by offering Canadians greater encouragement to invest in competition with Americans in this resource development.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This again is one of those decisions that might have been any other percentage. However, an attempt was made to
Income Tax Act
determine what we considered was the proper percentage which a company under these conditions might have by way of a reserve at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada. Whether 3 per cent was correct, or whether it should be 2, 4 or 5 per cent, I could not say, but I am recommending 3 per cent. I believe that on the whole it will be found acceptable to those who felt that there should be a reserve of this kind.
With respect to the second part of the question, I think it has reference to the words at the bottom of page 22. This is a most complicated section which I think leads one to think at first reading that possibly there would be no reserve. The purpose is to permit one to have a reserve of 3 per cent building up at the rate of one-twelfth per year which I think presupposes that there would always be some reserve.

In connection with the accounts receivable part of this long section, representations have been made to me which I wish to read to the committee because I think it would be possible administratively to deal with this discrimination-I think it could be called that-however unintentional. This reads:
Resolution No. 8 of the proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act reads as follows:
"8. That for the 1955 and subsequent taxation years proceeds of a sale or realization of inventory or accounts receivable of a taxpayer upon or after selling or ceasing to carry on a business be included in computing income, but that the taxpayer be given the option of paying tax in respect thereof at his average rate of tax for the three taxation years immediately preceding the year in which he sold or ceased to carry on the business."
For an individual the ''taxation year" is the calendar year, in which case this resolution would only apply to transactions made after December 31, 1954, whereas in the case of a corporation the "taxation year" is the fiscal period, so that as presently worded the resolution could apply to transactions of the nature contemplated which had taken place in 1954, depending on the date of its fiscal year end.
One case has come to my notice of a company with February 28 as its year end, where the major portion of the business including inventories was disposed of during the summer of 1954, with the transaction being completed strictly in accordance with the income tax regulations then in force.
It may be claimed that a corporation's taxation year would end when it ceased to do business, upon the sale of its inventory or accounts receivable, but this would not hold if it had other revenue producing property, such as securities, which had not been disposed of until 1955. Consequently, if the sale of inventory or accounts receivable took place during a fiscal year which ended after December 31, 1954, the corporation could be required to include the proceeds in income, whereas if the fiscal year coincided with the calendar year the corporation would not be affected by the proposed resolution, even though the sale had been made on the same day in both cases.

Income Tax Act
The resolution as now submitted would therefore appear to be discriminatory not only as between individuals and corporations, but between corporations with different year ends. In addition, the retroactive feature could prove a real hardship in many cases.
It could be that it was not the minister's intention to make this legislation both retroactive and discriminatory and I am wondering if you would care to raise these points when the resolution in question comes up for discussion before the house in committee.
It seems to me that there is substantial discrimination and I am wondering if it could not be met by providing a fixed date and not referring it to the phrase "taxation year", which I think quite obviously could introduce great inequalities which are not intended.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sure the representations which have been made to my hon. friend cover some of the awkwardness created by the adoption of the present section. Nevertheless it has been our custom to apply laws during the taxation year and the discrimination which my hon. friend speaks of is discrimination which, if it exists, exists on every occasion when you make a change of this kind. While I recognize the possibility that some person will be taxed while another person may not be, I think that is one of those things that we will have to face when we meet it.

I am not seeking to argue against the general principle which the minister has just mentioned. One or two other things have been stood over for consideration and I wonder if the minister would not just take a look at this to find out whether it would really hurt the public interest if this were done. He has admitted that there is discrimination; in effect he says it is the rub of the green and you cannot get away from it. Actually he did not say that you cannot get away from the very points I am raising. Would not the minister consider whether in fact this could or could not be done, perhaps without any injury to the public interest and certainly with a view to removing what could be great hardships to individual institutions.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

I have another point which I wish to raise, and I do not know whether the minister has an amendment up his sleeve to cover this one as well. I would be glad if he would certify that the amendment was offered only because of my representations, but I expect that that is asking too much. I want to raise the whole question of changing the character of accounts receivable and inventories in the case of transactions such as those we have been discussing. I take it that this is legislation to nullify the effect of certain judgments of the income tax appeal board and I should like to refer briefly to one or two of those judgments and ask for further elucidation of the change. I refer first to No. 10 v. Minister of National Revenue, 3 Tax Appeal Board Cases, 367, where we find the following:
At the request of counsel for the appellant, this appeal was heard in camera. The point involved is the taxation, in the appellant's 1946 income tax assessment, of an amount of $9,147.32 as a profit on the sale of the appellant's inventory in a business which had been carried on by him since 1901 until it was sold In the fall of the year 1945.
The appellant, who was a sole proprietor, had another business of a similar nature which he conducted in another city, and which he had commenced at a date much later than the business with which we are concerned in this appeal.
The appellant's evidence was that, in the fall of the year 1945, he decided to sell the complete business which he conducted in the city in which he resided at that time. A buyer was found, and an agreement was entered into in September, 1945, between the appellant and the purchaser, a copy of which was filed as an exhibit. The agreement recites the sale and specifies that the consideration shall be the aggregate of:
"(a) The price of the aforesaid stock in trade as of November 1, 1945, determined as hereinafter set out, and
(b)	Accounts receivable at the rate of eighty-five cents (.85<0 on the dollar, and
(c)	Five thousand dollars ($5,000) for the fixtures and equipment hereinbefore referred to."
I need not read the details, but I shall read the judgment as follows:
I am satisfied that the amount in question herein was not derived as a profit from the carrying on of business, but was derived, upon the cessation of business, as an appreciation of capital, which is not taxable under the Income War Tax Act.
Having reached this decision, it is unnecessary to deal with the problem of the valuation of the inventory which was raised at the hearing, other than to say that the method of valuation of the inventory in previous years had been accepted by the minister's officials and, in my opinion, if a change in the method of valuing the inventory was to be adopted at the time of the sale in the fall

of 1945, the same method of valuation would have to be adopted for the opening inventory at the commencement of the fiscal period of the business ending in 1945.
I do not think I need to read the other case.
I think the principle is clear, and the steps which are now being taken to alter the practice and principle which has been followed are also clear. I wish the minister would say something as to the equity of the proceedings. Some people say there is no equity in income tax, but I believe there is. I should like to hear something said on that because it is a drastic change in the operation of the law as it stood and in what was considered at that time to be an equitable arrangement as between the taxpayer and the Minister of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member has made just as good a case for this change as he made for the proposed amendment that I had ready when he spoke. He has read the judgment of the court setting out the reason why inventories in that particular instance escaped taxation. It must be obvious that the reason given was that this gentleman was no longer carrying on business, and the law as it stood at that time was that what was taxable was what one earned in carrying on a business. In those circumstances we are changing it so that these items may now be taxable even if the business ceases to be in the hands of the taxpayer or in fact if it ceases to exist altogether. Under those circumstances I think he will agree with me-in fact, I know from the words he has used he does-that it would be fair to other taxpayers that this profit which has in fact been made, though not realized while the business has been carried on, should be taxable.

Is it quite clear that in every case this is a profit in the proper sense of the word? I can understand that in some cases it may be, but in other cases it may well be what the income tax appeal board found it to be in these several cases extending over a period of several years, namely an accretion on capital. The feature of this bill, introducing quite extensive new legislation into the Income Tax Act, that concerns me is that it proceeds on the blanket assumption that every appreciation in inventory in the case of sale or other disposal of the business in which it has been earned, and is later realized, is necessarily profit. It seems to me that an assumption as broad as that is too broad to be justified. As I say, I can see some cases where it may be felt that increases in inventory value should be treated as profit, but I must say that I feel some allergy toward treating as income what has been hitherto
Income Tax Act
treated, and in this case by the courts, as simply an accretion to capital. Every step we take to turn into profit what has been treated by the courts in sound decisions as capital represents the equivalent of another march towards increase in taxation, engulfing in the scope of income tax things that have not been regarded in their proper meaning as income hitherto.
By what reason does the minister say that in every such case what has hitherto been held by the courts to be an accretion to capital should from this point on be regarded as profit and treated as income?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps I did not make myself clear. I understand the case my hon. friend has referred to won on the ground that, because the business had ceased to be in existence, therefore certain consequences followed, and did not specifically state that any increased value of an inventory was an increase in capital as such. If that were the decision, I suggest it would not be founded on any of the philosophies of taxation that have been followed in the past, because the purpose of the income tax is to tax a business in which a profit is being sought, that is, certain profits that are earned in a business. When a trader carries an inventory, he is changing the inventory daily, he hopes, turning it over as often as he can, for the purpose of making a profit. The inventory is not his capital; it is the means of earning his income.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to pursue what the hon. member for Eglinton has said, because it seems to me that what we are trying to tax is income. As he has pointed out, we have had a board with the authority to look into the facts and determine what was and what was not income, and we have had a few cases here, and there are several others with which the minister is no doubt familiar, where in fact the board has come to the conclusion that it was not income but capital. Now, what is happening is that we are getting away from what I think is the fair thing, that is the attempt to find what is income and what is not income. What we are saying in the statute is that such and such a transaction, even though under the fair interpretation it is in the contemplation of the law not income at all, yet by the wording we put into the statute it becomes income. I wonder if this is a sound decision. Do we want to introduce measures to tax capital profits? That is another matter. My colleague says, "I hope we never come to it". So do I. But I only say this seems an indirect way of getting to that. Is it fair to go behind a competent

Income Tax Act
board which is charged with the duty, among other things, of finding out what income is?-and presumably it is competent tb do that. After all, transactions vary from case to case. Two transactions may look exactly alike, and yet it may well be that one transaction that takes place shows an accretion to income and another one does not. What we are doing here seems to me to be regrettable, stepping in and undertaking to vary by the arbitrary power of the law the meaning of words which have a definite meaning in the business transactions, and which we have a competent board to assess.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I must say that I am astonished at the principle which my hon. friend has tried to elucidate. Surely parliament aims to make the law for the very purpose of raising the revenues that are required. If it is found that parliament does not agree with the results of decisions which are made by the income tax appeal board, surely he is not suggesting that we should stop all legislative processes at that point.
It may be that we are making such a great change in what has been the accepted practice heretofore that my hon. friend would feel obliged to object to it on the ground of public policy. But as I understand the scope of the income tax appeal board, it is to rule on cases which come before them, by way of interpretation of the act, as to whether the taxpayer is exempt or is taxable and so on. It is then the duty of parliament, I would think, to pass legislation consequent upon its decisions if they feel that public policy requires that to be done. That is just the point here. We are in fact legislating as the consequence of a decision, and we feel that legislation should commend itself to the committee. Indeed, I think it does.
I suppose my argument can be summed up by saying that what you are really doing is saying that A is not A, but is B. But the legislature can do that, I assume.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What we are saying is that certain things shall be considered as income which a decision of the income tax appeal board said was not income.

The minister has not yet dealt -certainly not to my satisfaction-with the points I sought to raise. Of course, I agree that you must have general rules in situations of this kind. I am concerned, however, about the effect this legislation may have. The minister is seeking to carry out what he conceives to be sound public policy in asking parliament to declare to be income that which

has hitherto been found by the courts not to be income but to be capital or an increase or accretion to capital.
Such reasons as the minister has given- and there have not been many of them-seem to me not to go beyond saying this: in some cases it may be fair that the taxpayer should not be permitted to reap the full benefit from the accretion to his capital, as the courts have regarded the transaction up to the present time, where he goes out of business or sells his business. But if parliament steps in now and legislates in the manner in which we are being invited to legislate in clause 27, thereby introducing into the Income Tax Act some extensive and far-reaching new provisions- indeed, about four pages of legislation-I should be greatly surprised if we are not legislating to create as many injustices as we are being invited to remove.
That is the difficulty that invariably arises. I think the minister will appreciate the force of the point we are trying to make here. No one denies that parliament has the right, in proper cases, to legislate so as to change the law as declared by the courts or by the income tax appeal board. Parliament often does that. But here we are dealing with a situation which has many ramifications. It is hard for us sitting here this afternoon to conceive of all the circumstances that may arise in the case of either the sale of a business in which there is an inventory-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is so with respect to every amendment in the whole act.

Yes. But here you are dealing with cases of an involved nature, with an unquestioned wide variety of circumstances. It seems to me that to step in and treat them all as though they yielded to a simple formula, namely that what has been declared by the courts hitherto as being capital shall hereafter in every case regardless of the circumstances be treated as income and subject to taxation, is inevitably going to result in as many injustices as we are now being invited to remove, and perhaps even more of them.
I cannot approach a matter of this kind without serious misgivings as to the effect of legislation of this nature that is just overriding a decision of the courts; and it is overriding not just one decision but a whole course of judicial decisions. The first of this group of cases was decided by the income tax appeal board in February, 1951. That was over four years ago. The decisions run right down to later cases. The first was No. 10 v. Minister of National Revenue. Then there was one later in 1951, that of Empire Manufacturing Company Limited v. Minister of

National Revenue. Then this year again we have another decision of the income tax appeal board, in the case of Nemessany v. Minister of National Revenue, which again confirmed the same decision. So that we have a whole course of judicial decisions on this point. Now we are being asked to reverse completely the law as declared in a whole course of judicial decisions. I must say that I approach this matter with extremely grave misgivings as to the effect of the legislation we are now being invited to pass.

It is considered that the existing wording of the bill does not adequately cover the situation where deemed-to-be dividends are received by a non-resident. The existing wording refers to dividends "required by this act to be included in computing the recipient's income ..." but the Canadian Income Tax Act does not require these dividends to be included in a non-resident's income. For this reason this amendment adds the words:
"or that would be so required if the recipient were resident in Canada at the time the dividends were so deemed to have been received".
I will ask my colleague the Minister of National Revenue to move that amendment.

That Bill 417, an act to amend the Income Tax Act, be amended by striking out lines 44 to 46 on page 24 thereof and substituting therefor the following:
"and that are required by this act to be included in computing the recipient's income (or that would be so required if the recipient were resident in Canada at the time the dividends were so deemed to have been received) shall be deemed to have been paid by the payer corporation."

I am not sure that I have taken in the full import of the amendment. What I should like to do is ask the minister at this point whether he can assure the committee that the effect of this section as amended is not to tax the income of charitable trusts and corporations in any circumstance. It appears to me that a reading of the section as it stood indicates that although no tax is levied on charitable trusts or corporations as such, a tax of 15 per cent is levied on the income which comes to the charitable trusts. If that is so, then in effect the passing of this amendment will reduce charitable funds in the hands of these trusts by 15 per cent of the income which comes from certain dividends. Before proceeding further, I should like to have the minister give the departmental interpretation of the effect of this section in those cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The purpose of the amendment was not to tax charitable corporations, and it does not do so. It might be said it taxes the income of charitable corporations in the sense that income is received from any other corporation which is now being taxed, but that is true probably of the income of charitable organizations because most of it is subject to taxation in one form or another before it is received.

Then my fears are well founded, because what we have here is a new tax of 15 per cent on income devoted to charitable purposes, and which would not be taxable in that way if this amendment were not passed. I ask the minister if he is not catching more fish in this net than was intended, because it is a broad section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I suggest to my hon. friend that he knows exactly the purpose of this section, and it is not intended to go beyond that.

As I understand the reply I have had so far, there is a tax of 15 per cent

Income Tax Act
which will be levied which is not now levied on dividends received by charitable trusts in certain cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, the tax is on the payment of dividends by another corporation.
I appreciate that, but it is on the payment of dividends to a charitable trust, if the charitable trust chooses to take the dividends in this form.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Of course.

The effect of that, Mr. Chairman, will be to reduce the income of charitable trusts, in some cases, because to the extent the 15 per cent tax has to be paid there will be that much less income for the trust. As the minister knows, these dividends which are taxable are dividends paid by corporations whose issued shares are largely owned by a charitable trust. I suppose the Atkinson foundation, which owns the issued shares of the Toronto Daily Star, might be one such. If I am correct in my interpretation of this section, then the net income from the Toronto Daily Star which is available to the Atkinson foundation will be reduced by 15 per cent which is taken as a tax under that section. I would ask the minister to tell me if I am correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am not familiar with the terms, assets or liabilities of the Atkinson foundation.

Well, assume that a charitable trust, the Atkinson foundation, holds the controlling issued shares and that the earnings of the newspaper are designated income within the meaning of the act. It may be that the effect of subsection 6 is to save those companies where the shares were received for trust as a bequest under a will, and I think that is the effect of that subsection. But where those shares were obtained in other cases by purchase or by investment and the portfolio of the charitable trust comes within the section, certainly the income of the organization which produced the revenue for the charity would be reduced by that amount. That is the point I want clearly understood when we accept this.

Has the minister answered the question of the hon. member for St. Paul's? Is there not a point there with which he might wish to deal, if we could agree on exactly what it is? Surely the illustration of the Atkinson foundation is very practical, and the result might be what is suggested. Supposing that is the effect; would the minister then be quite happy to take this stand as against charitable foundations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am, as I said before, unfamiliar with the operations of the Atkinson foundation.
We will take that as an illustration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Taking that as an illustration, and assuming that it is a charitable organization with an investment in another company -are those the facts with which we are dealing at the moment? Then I would suppose, Mr. Chairman, that they should not be in any preferred position with respect to a non-resident corporation, for example, or a trader or dealer with respect to the object of this section, which is to collect a tax which at the moment is not being collected.

That may be one view of the effect of this section, but another view is that this is doing indirectly and in a roundabout fashion what the government and the house would not want to do directly, and that is to impose a 15 per cent toll on funds which are mainly directed to charitable purposes. Unless they are mainly directed to charitable purposes they do not come under the section at all. When I say "mainly directed", I mean to the extent that the majority of the issued shares of the earning company are held by the charitable trust. The same thing would apply to other exempt organizations in section 62 of the act, such as labour organizations, non-profit organizations and so on. However, I do not see how any instance of that would arise. Certainly there might be very serious inroads made on charitable funds if this section is allowed to stand.

Would the minister not agree that if you had a situation where in fact a charitable trust was going to bear the whole effect of this tax, that would be a case for consideration? After all, we do a good deal to protect charitable foundations. I quite agree that you cannot have every company, a portion of whose shares are owned by a charitable foundation, exempted from the act. I would think there may be some special cases, however.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Carry that one step forward to a provision of this kind, which provides for a tax on dividends paid by a company which is controlled by a tax-exempt organization; that is what we are discussing. If my hon. friend agrees that where they own shares in a corporation that corporation should not be tax exempt, then I suggest it would be even more so where they control the corporation.

I am coming back to the case outlined. I am not familiar with the details of it, except in a general way, and I do not know what the technical position is.

I listened to what my hon. friend from St. Paul's said, and it seemed to me that the net effect of his explanation meant that in this case the tax was going to come wholly out of the income devoted to charitable purposes. If I misunderstood it, then my argument falls to the ground. If that is the situation, is it not possible, by a word, to deal with it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The advantage which is given to a charitable organization is given with respect to its income. There is an exemption with respect to the income of charitable organizations. But I do not think anyone would seriously suggest there ought to be a further exemption of income received from corporations which would be tax exempt. That is what would happen if we did not have this legislation. It provides for a tax on a dividend account, for a controlled corporation, to certain other persons. At the moment it is not being taxed, and that is why we are trying to tax it.

It would be a simple matter if there were intent to preserve the position of the charitable trusts. I raise this point because it seems to me that although charitable trusts are not being taxed directly, they would have to be kept in a preferred position to achieve the result I have in mind. It seems to me that if this section is allowed to pass it will discourage to a considerable extent the payment of dividends to charitable trusts; because the payer corporations will have to provide 15 per cent tax with respect to dividends payable to a charitable trust, whereas, as the law now stands, the payer corporation does not have to provide that tax at all. And it is not put to the expense simply because some of its shares, or a large part of its shares, are held by what is a charitable trust.
The situation could be remedied if under subsection 1(b), where reference is made to a person exempt from tax under section 62, a charitable trust or charity under section 62 were excluded.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

Perhaps we could more profitably discuss this elsewhere, because I do not think there is a meeting of minds at all. What we are trying to do is deal with a situation where a tax-exempt organization controls another corporation, and the latter then distributes dividends to the former. We feel that should be taxable, and nothing I have heard this afternoon has changed my mind on that point. The normal purpose of a charity is not to go around acquiring the control of corporations. There may be reasons for doing so, but I think for taxation purposes we ought to consider those reasons.
