Mr. Speaker, I too would like to lend my support to the previous speakers in asking that further consideration be given to the question of a refund to motor car dealers. It is true that this reduction has meant a stimulus to their business, but on the other hand it is a direct loss for which they will in no way be able to be repaid. There is one other thing I should like to mention in connection with the excise tax on cars. It happens that I have had some experience as a car dealer, and comparing them with other commodities on which this tax is levied I have noticed that there is quite a difference.
The car dealer is possibly one of the few retailers who deal directly with the manufacturer, whereas in the case of other commodities the tax is paid first by the distributor and then it becomes a part of that distributor's base price. When he sets up his price to the wholesaler, of course, there is a margin of profit on that total base price, including the excise tax. The same thing happens between the wholesaler and the retailer and, of course, the retailer does likewise. So by the time the retailer pays the tax it has possibly pyramided by another 50 per cent, or maybe 100 per cent in some cases.
The car dealer is in the unhappy position that he pays the full amount of the tax before he takes possession of a new car, and he has to hold it in his possession after paying out the money including the tax. When it is sold to the consumer he has not made five cents

Therefore it will be readily seen that this is unfair to the car dealer and certainly not in keeping with merchandising methods as followed by other dealers in taxable goods. Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words regarding this. I quite agree with what has been said regarding the social welfare organizations. I should also like to say this in regard to the tax on cars that were held by the dealers when the budget came down. In some cases it did not amount to very much, but in other cases it amounted to a great deal. We have to remember that despite the fact that 5 per cent was taken off the 15 per cent excise tax, 10 per cent still remains, plus a 10 per cent sales tax. That is a great deal of money to pay on a car, especially when a car is an essential item to the worker of today. I know many workers who have to use a car every day to go to work. In fact I had a worker up to see me last Sunday night who had to travel 27J miles to work each day. Not only is he paying the excise tax and the sales tax; he is also paying, of course, the gasoline tax.
One other subject I should like to mention is the fact that in the budget this year the minister did not do anything regarding the excise tax on cigarettes. I know that the smuggling of cigarettes, though reduced to some extent on account of the slight reduction in the excise tax in 1953, is carried on today on a large scale despite everything the Royal Canadian Mounted Police can do. The smuggling benefits only one person, the smuggler, but he benefits at the expense of the smoker, the government and the manufacturer. There is only one solution to the problem, and that is for the government to reduce the tax differential as between Canada and the United States so it would not be profitable for the smuggler to take a chance on bringing those cigarettes into Canada.

Excise Tax Act
On the 1st of April I came across a case where king size cigarettes were smuggled into Canada, and I know the price the particular party paid for them. I wondered why king size cigarettes were not sold in Canada. King size cigarettes are manufactured and sold in practically every other country in the world. On T.V. programs that we receive in Canada from United States stations, king size cigarettes are shown and advertised very extensively.
When I inquired into this matter I found that the excise tax on Canadian-manufactured cigarettes runs to about 18 cents for a package of 20. To qualify under this tax rate the cigarettes must not weigh more than 2J pounds per 1,000 cigarettes. I understand that includes paper. All king size cigarettes weigh more than that. If king size cigarettes were manufactured in Canada they would attract another tax of about 2J cents per package. As king size cigarettes require more tobacco, material and labour, the cost to the consumer in Canada of king size cigarettes would be an extra 3 to 4 cents a package.
There is only one remedy for this; that is, that Canada do what is done in the United States and allow the tax to be the same for king size as for ordinary cigarettes. In order to stop this smuggling, the differential in the tax as between Canada and the United States must be reduced. From what I know, smuggling now is nearly as great as it was in 1953.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with those who have already spoken on behalf of the automobile dealers urging that a rebate be made to the dealers who had already paid the 5 per cent excise tax which was reduced by the government in the latest budget.
I have here a letter written to me by a dealer in my own riding. I should like to read it because I think it explains the case of the automobile dealers very well indeed. It is written by Mr. George Hogan, president of Hogan motors, Danforth avenue, Toronto. The letter reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Hees:
Confirming our telephone conversation of April 15th, I am pleased to submit certain information respecting the effect of the recent reduction in excise tax on automobiles. While I know that this subject is one of considerable concern to dealers generally across Canada, I can speak most accurately with respect to our own dealership, and the losses which we have suffered on automobiles in our inventory as of April 5th, 1955.
At the time of the effective date of the excise tax reduction we had in stock one hundred and fifty-three new cars. The 5 per cent portion of the excise tax already paid on that inventory amounts to approximately $15,384. In addition we, of course, had in our inventory a comparable stock of used cars on which we must absorb a comparable loss. We are satisfied that our position is reasonably representative of many automobile dealers, not only in our own metropolitan area, but across all provinces of Canada. A large number of those are larger dealerships than our own and, of course, many are smaller but we believe it is reasonable to claim that all dealers regardless of size will suffer losses somewhat proportionate to our own.
Excise Tax Act
Like most Canadian dealers we appreciate the tax reduction as an indication that automobiles are being partially removed from the category of luxury goods for tax purposes. However, it appears far from equitable that a tax which ostensibly was imposed on the consumer should now be levied against us as "collectors-in-advance" and for which we now have absolutely no hope of being reimbursed except by rebate from the government.
As you are aware automobiles are paid for or financed when they leave the factory door. Dealers must not only pay the tax in full but, in many cases, must absorb finance and insurance charges on them until they are sold. Because of the time of year which the budget is presented, dealers are obligated to carry possibly their heaviest inventories of the entire year. If they, in fear of an impending budget, radically reduce inventories, they may lessen their losses through tax reduction without rebate but materially reduce their sales at a time when they should be most adequately stocked.
It has been frequently argued that in the past, when tax increases were applied, the dealers were permitted to take advantage of the situation and pass that increase on to the consumer. This has not been our experience nor do we believe that it has been the practice of most dealers. In fact, during most periods of past tax increases, dealers' stocks have been extremely limited in size.
Because the tax is collected at the manufacturer's level it is probably one of the easiest and cheapest to collect. The question of refund of tax could be just as easily handled and I would suggest one of two methods listed below-
1.	The factories could refund the amount of reduction in tax on all cars delivered by the factory from March 1st to budget date and bill the government.
2.	The factories could refund the amount of reduction in tax on all cars in dealers' hands on budget date and bill the government.
I should appreciate your study of our problem because, as intimated earlier, I think we are fairly representative of the dealer body across the country. Whatever you may be able to do to draw to the attention of the government this manifestly unfair situation will be greatly appreciated.
Yours very truly,
Hogan Pontiac Buick Ltd.
G. W. Hogan, President.
I think that outlines in very clear terms exactly the problem these dealers are up against.

I suggest to hon. members that when they consider the problem in that light, desirable though it might be to aid charitable organizations in this or any other respect, they will come to the conclusion that any aid granted could be granted in some other way that would be less costly or less troublesome to deal with.
Then on the second point, as to the motor car dealers, I realize that hon. members have had representations made to them by almost every dealer in their own constituencies, and by the various associations in the several provinces. And there could not be any doubt that this may result in some loss to motor car dealers. When I have said that, I have said it as a possibility; I do not admit that it is a probability. It is much easier to stop thinking with the situation on April 5 than it is to go on to consider what it has been since.
It is quite true that motor car dealers had in their inventories on that day a number of used and new motor cars, on the latter of which a tax had been paid. Just to multiply the tax by the number of motor cars, and come to the ready conclusion that the loss sustained by motor car dealers was a result of the multiplication of those two figures should not, I suggest, be accepted by hon. members quite so readily. There is no certainty whatever that a motor car dealer took a loss on a motor car which he had in his possession on April 5.
I do not think that is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Permit me to continue. It may very well have happened and, as I said at the beginning, it probably did happen. But I say now that it should not be assumed that it happened in every case and on every car.
The result is that in computing the possible loss, one must just assume that there was a maximum loss, and then say whether in fact there was that result. No one has mentioned the cost of the refund which has been recommended to the government by various members. We really have had no way of computing that, either. But I think the gross loss, if I may put it that way, by taking the tax paid on the cars on hand on April 5, regardless of the subsequent dealings those cars might have gone through, might have run somewhere between $2 and $3 million.
Hon members are saying in effect that motor car dealers should be dealt with in a manner different from any other retailers or any other persons who, on the face of it,

Excise Tax Act
suffer a loss because of budgetary action. It has not been the custom of this parliament to give rebates and refunds consequent upon budgetary action. The whole purpose, or almost the whole purpose, of the secrecy which attends budgetary announcements is to avoid any possible suggestion that one could make a profit, or escape a loss, or something like that, because of a change in taxation laws which, as all know, are made effective after the close of business on budget day.
If you were to single out the motor car dealers and say they should be reimbursed by the government or by the taxpayers of Canada to the extent of their ostensible losses on that date, I am sure you would find that your problem would increase immensely, and that you would be faced with similar problems at every change in the tax laws of the country.
This may not sound like very good comfort, however, for the motor car dealers who feel they have taken a direct retail loss. But let me point out what has been referred to by more than one speaker today, that the motor car dealers along with the motor car trade, and along with almost every business group, as well as innumerable individuals, urged this government to reduce the excise tax on motor cars, and did this several months before the budget was brought down. Speeches were made in the house by persons who suggested that if that tax were reduced, or removed, there would be such a stimulation in the motor car trade that not only would the economy revive but that indeed the loss the government would be contemplating through the reduction in the tax would be more than made up by the increased sales of motor cars during the coming fiscal year.
On the night of the budget I believe I said our loss from the reduction in the excise tax we did make would probably be about $26 million. Now if in fact, as a result of the increased sale of motor cars, we had no net loss, and the $26 million was made up by the reduced tax on the increased sales, how can anyone suggest that the motor car dealers would not have a profitable year?
I am not suggesting that will be the outcome; but I am saying that under the circumstances, and because it is not such a clear case of direct loss in the number of dollars paid by way of tax on the motor car, I do not feel that we could depart from the past practice of not making refunds under these circumstances. And if I were to add a postscript it would be that if hon. members felt there ought to be a reduction in the sales tax on an item, as a matter of logic one would expect that anyone who had that article on

his shelf in a retail store would expect a refund of the amount of the tax that had been paid.
If stated in that manner it would draw the attention of hon. members to one of two things. Either they feel that because of the large sum of money which has been paid by way of tax on the motor car-that is, $75 and up, or something like that

as compared with the smaller amount that would be paid by the retailer in some other line, the motor car dealer had a special case for special consideration which would not be given to anyone else on that account; or, alternatively, I think they would feel, as we do, that much as we do not want to impose any loss on anyone as the result of action we take here, nevertheless, it would be unwise to take the step suggested in this particular case.
At least two speakers have mentioned my remarks on May 18, I believe it was, in answer to the hon. member for Kamloops. I do not think on that occasion I was doing more than promising continued consideration of this problem. Indeed, since that time I have received a deputation from the motor car dealers' association of Canada, and have received from them a great deal of information on which to base my judgment. And that is precisely what I meant. I knew perfectly well that we would have these representations after the budget announcement was made, and I did not expect the house would suppose that I would categorically refuse to consider any information made available in the future. I do not intend to do so from now on, either, for that matter. But to say that because I did not on that occasion deny that there would be further consideration, it could be read as a promise that I would give favourable consideration, seems to me to be stretching the point far beyond either what was intended or what could be read into what was said.
I would like to think we could find a way of avoiding this situation. It has been said that the budget comes at the worst possible time for the motor car dealer; that is, at the time of the spring build-up of his inventory. There must be a lot of other retail businesses in Canada which find that February, March or April, or whatever the month may be, is the period when they have as high an inventory as they have at any other time. But of course I agree that the motor car dealers do, in fact, find that the budget comes at an awkward time with relation to their inventory.
They have made representations as to how this problem could have been overcome. We were not able to accept those recommendations, not because there was not some merit in them but because we did not feel they met

the problem quite in the manner it should be met, if any change could be effected. I can only say, sir, without anything possibly being read into what I may say in the future, I would hope that some means can be devised whereby there will be a minimum of loss on any occasion when there is a change in the tax laws of Canada.
If I have not covered all the points that were brought up in the course of discussion I shall be glad to do so if I can be reminded of them.

What about
cigarettes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member for Peterborough referred to the tax on cigarettes. We studied the tax on cigarettes, and I rather thought that answering my hon. friend at this time would be to really take part in the budget debate again, because he did not take time to do so on that occasion. He made a point about smuggling. I was informed at the time we were giving this consideration that smuggling was not now quite the problem that it had been some three or four years ago. Nevertheless it is a problem, and we do not want to do anything which would aggravate it. On the contrary, we feel that the less there is it is not only the better for the revenue of the people of Canada, but the better from the point of view of a more law-abiding citizenry. At the same time it is not the problem which was pressing upon the government when they altered the tax some three years ago, I think it was. I would hope that any future change in the tax law would not have to be dictated by that reason.
What about king size cigarettes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On that point I am afraid I have not much information. I am not familiar with king size or any other size.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would the minister care to comment on the question of extending sales tax exemption to a longer list of drugs and medicines?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I omitted that. I received representations from several drug associations and medical associations with respect to tax exemptions on various drugs. It seemed to me that we had embarked upon a tax exemption out of sympathy for those who have to use specific drugs for particular diseases. While that was probably laudable and understandable and there were some cases, of course, where the cost of the drug was of such magnitude that it would normally drain the resources of a family with average income and for that reason ought to be given special consideration, it also seemed
Excise Tax Act
to me there was not, if I might use the words, any philosophy behind this as to the general approach to tax exemption for drugs as such. I agree with my hon. friend that we ought to have a review of the whole problem. While he has added the words "for the purpose of extending the exemptions", I would not go that far, but I would go so far as to say that a study would probably give us an accurate picture of those drug exemptions which should be granted, as I have said, for the reason that their cost is so great in that it would interfere with the normal savings or income of a family.
The other group of diseases that are sought to be cured are of a kind that we would like to do what we could to overcome; but in any event those normal, everyday drugs, patent medicines and the like are perhaps not ot that particular class. A general study-and I may be using words which probably could be much better interpreted by my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare- along this line with a review of all the drug items would be useful, and I think probably would be profitable in the sense that the house would have a chance of approving or disapproving the choice which was made after the general study.

I have one question on the automobile tax. The minister said that in the past it had not been the practice of the government to refund excise tax after the budget was brought down. Is it not correct that back in 1921, when precisely the same circumstances arose, the government ultimately did refund the tax to the automobile dealers, I believe some seven years later? I believe when they did it they also paid the back interest. I am just wondering whether that would not be a precedent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If we can go into committee of the whole I shall answer the questions, Mr. Speaker.

On clause 1:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I just answer the question asked by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. It is a fact that the excise tax on motor cars which was reduced in the summer of 1920 was refunded in the year 1927; but we have had several reductions in excise tax on motor cars since that time and no refunds have been made. I was referring, of course, to the later practice rather than that of 35 years ago.

I was amazed at the statement made by the Minister of Finance just

Excise Tax Act
now in closing the debate on second reading with respect to the intended effect of the statement he made in the house on May 18. He has indicated what he did not intend to convey to the house or to the motor car dealers who, through their associations, were making representations to him seeking refund of the tax paid on cars purchased by them prior to the introduction of the budget. He indicated that he intended only to convey the idea that this was a matter under consideration; he just was not closing the door, and it was a sort of routine matter.
Mr. Chairman, I do not know how the minister could have been so careless with his words. Let us remember that this matter had already been discussed. It had been discussed very thoroughly in the course of the budget debate. Those same considerations had been very directly laid before the minister then. A number of hon. members had put the question very directly to the minister, and it was in the minds of all hon. members; it was recognized to be a problem to which no little difficulty was attached for the very reasons given by the minister this afternoon, because it does raise questions about where you draw the line. It was not because of any lack of warning that the minister allowed himself to say those things on May 18, which certainly have had the effect of misleading the motor car dealers involved. Let me read again the question that gave rise to the minister's statement. On page 3881 of Hansard the hon. member for Kamloops asked this question:
I should like to ask the Minister of Finance if he has received a brief from the motor car dealers' association of British Columbia asking for his consideration of their request for a refund of the excise taxes paid on cars in stock on April 5? Would the minister say whether he will be able to give further and favourable consideration to this admittedly difficult problem, and whether he is able to hold out any encouragement to that association?
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that everything is in the question; the whole problem is set forth there. There is an indication that the questioner recognized the difficulties involved. He asks whether the minister is prepared to give further and favourable consideration to the problem. He is then asked whether he is prepared to give encouragement to those who have made those submissions. It cannot be said that anything was omitted from the question or that any hidden meaning was left lurking. That was a question that was open and plain and gave the minister complete warning. To this question the minister gave this answer:
I received briefs not only from the British Columbia motor car dealers' association but from the national body, I think from all the provincial bodies, and from quite a number of individual

dealers. Of course we accept these representations along with all others and give them our best consideration.
But the hon. member for Kamloops did not stop there. That might have been regarded as just a routine answer to a question. The hon. member continued:
Consideration is always welcome, but how about encouragement?
The hon. member went right back to the very nub of the question, and then the Minister of Finance permitted himself to utter these words:
Encouragement is a word which I think is used on every occasion by this government as to its intentions with respect to the Canadian economy.
I am quite sure that hon. members of this house drew from those words the only interpretation that could properly be given to them, that the minister was seriously considering this request for refund and was indicating that there was in his thinking some reason for encouragement. Why otherwise did the minister go on and talk about encouragement being in the mind of the government in relation to the Canadian economy. There is no doubt at all about the meaning the motor car dealers drew from those words.
What I said earlier I now repeat, that if the minister did not intend to give effect to their requests for a refund in some form, then he should not have used words like those. He should have been clear and direct for the purpose I mentioned when I spoke on this matter on June 2.
Just after the minister made this remark one hon. member of this house made a comment to me to the effect that that was not the kind of answer his predecessor would have given. If it was not in the mind of the Minister of Finance to give effect to this request, if the Minister of Finance saw in the way these formidable difficulties to which he has drawn attention this afternoon, then at that time he owed it to the house and to these motor car dealers who were concerned and who were making representations to say that he was sorry, that he would give the best consideration he could to the matter, but the difficulties were so formidable that he could not hold out any hope. He should have told the motor car dealers they must accept the situation, that there would be no refund.
But the minister had not learned how to deal with questions of that kind in that way. I wish to say in all fairness that I hope there will not be a repetition of this sort of thing. Unquestionably the house and the motor car dealers right across Canada were misled by the words which the minister

allowed himself to use on that occasion into thinking there was some form of relief coming to them in response to their requests for a refund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I hope this will be my last word on this. There are two things that stand out. First of all, I was not as direct as my predecessor and I accept full responsibility for not saying that the facts of the matter were that before this question was asked I had been asked by the association of motor car dealers if I would reconsider the problem in the light of information which they would send to me. That information had not been received when the question was asked. My hon. friend could hardly expect me to get up in the house and say that my mind was made up, that I would not receive further information, that I would not consider further requests, that I would not see people who wanted to speak to me about this.
I had no intention whatever of suggesting in my answer that I was trying to be devious or to create an impression which was not in fact in my mind. Contrary to what my hon. friend says, no one has spoken to me about this before this afternoon, when it was raised by the hon. member for Eglin-ton. No one has said that my words indicated a favourable outcome to my consideration. No one has suggested that my words meant anything more than the kind of consideration you would expect a government to give to representations that had been made to it. I have not had a single dealer say he thought that my words meant the dealers were going to get a refund.
I think the minister has completely overlooked the discussion we had on this subject on June 2.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I know what my hon. friend said in the house on that occasion, but I repeat that I have never had anyone tell me they understood from that that they were going to get a refund. No one has approached me and said that was the case. The decision which had been announced on April 5 was still open for discussion, and that is as far as they must have gone.
Apparently my hon. friend feels that my answer was not a correct answer, that I should have said on that occasion that I would not receive further representations, that my mind was closed.

I do not wish to be unpleasant about this, but if at that time the minister had told the representatives of these dealers that he was giving consideration to their representations, I think any answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Kamloops should have been one in which he was
Excise Tax Act
more careful in the use of the word "encouragement" than he was on that occasion. He said:
Encouragement is a word which I think is used on every occasion by this government as to its intentions with respect to the Canadian economy.
It may be that the minister now regrets having used language like that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Not a bit.

Then I am surprised at the minister's present statement, because I do not know how he can assume now that his answer did not convey to those who heard it and to those who read it that there were grounds for feeling encouraged as to their hopes that some action was going to be taken by the minister in relation to their requests for refunds.

Mr. Chairman, I am not sure whether this is a question of privilege, but in connection with tobacco I have a letter here from a person who I think is well informed and who lives in the region down near the border where smuggling is being carried on. He makes the same objection as the hon. member for Peterborough. He says there is a terrific amount of smuggling which would be cured by a reduction in the tax. I put that before the government for consideration.

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 506, to amend the Customs Tariff.

Will any statement be
made on this?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, both at the resolution stage when the amendment was moved, and again when these items came up for discussion, there was a fairly full discussion, and each tariff change was considered seriatim.

I wish to make one or two remarks. I suppose it may be said that for almost 15 years we have had an extraordinary absence of tariff problems in this country. We had first of all the war, and then shortly after the war came the Geneva agreement, with GATT and all that it meant. As a result we have had comparatively little discussion on tariff matters. At the present time the situation is not as satisfactory as it has been. The Minister of Trade and Commerce came back from Geneva not too happy about the result.
Although it is perhaps fair to say that progress has been made since then under GATT, and that the situation is somewhat better, nevertheless we cannot say it is wholly satisfactory. For example, it is not satisfactory that up to the end of May our trade deficit with the world was $128 million, most of it, of course, with the United States. I talked the other day with a man recently back from Europe. Taking a long view of the next four or five years, he was greatly disturbed about our competitive position, for our manufacturers particularly, because of the tremendous energy and efficiency that he had seen, in Germany and in Switzerland particularly and elsewhere in Europe. He was asking himself what was going to be our position when

we had to face this competition, which he felt was becoming keener and keener.
At the present time our prosperity in Canada depends to a very substantial extent on huge capital investment, though also of course greatly on our trade. We must remember that in the long run our trade is tremendously important, an importance that it is impossible to exaggerate.
I come back for a moment to the situation vis-a-vis the United States. The United States administration has taken a broad view on trade matters, but has been handicapped and held back from time to time by congress. Therefore it is comforting to remind ourselves that quite recently the President was given by congress a considerable amount of scope and power in his own hands to reduce tariffs; not nearly as much as Roosevelt had at one time, but still much better than nothing.
We have in the tariff measure before us now very few changes. There are one or two increases in tariffs. Those came to us on the recommendation of the tariff board, which we respect. I hope perhaps this may relieve us from that hoary hypocrisy, from which we have suffered for so many years in this house, that the raising of the tariff is not a respectable thing to do and that no Liberal government ever does it. We have suffered from that for a long time. The government has really tried to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds. It has tried to be all things to all men, to face both ways at once, and to make the best of both worlds. I hope we may now be relieved of that. The increase I have particularly in mind, which affects fruit cocktail, comes to us recommended by a respectable source. I hope it may relieve us from being exposed to what I call a hoary hypocrisy.
It is satisfactory to be assured that the increases which are to be brought about have been agreed upon within the four corners of GATT, and we are encouraged in the hope that this useful organization may add further to the substantial measure of success it has had already. There is no doubt that GATT is aiming at the kind of world in which Canada can fare best but, on the other hand, we must try to look at each problem that comes up in a realistic and practical way. The changes which we are to have in the tariff act are, as I have said, moderate. I leave the matter now for the consideration of the sections.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word on this. I must say that this bill rather surprises me. I do not like its contents. I do not like the idea of raising tariffs, as we do in the

schedule; but more particularly I am wondering why the government is dealing with goods that may be subsidized within the country in the manner which this bill outlines.
This bill adopts a principle, it seems to me, which is quite wrong. It gives the governor in council the power to decide what duty shall be charged in order to offset the subsidy that may be granted in the country of origin of the goods. I do not want to quote the clause because it is not in order at this stage to do so, but in addition you have references	to	dumping. It	seems to
me that the government is taking backward steps in dealing with this whole problem of imports and tariffs.
If I understand the policy of the Liberal party as enunciated from time to time, it is	that we go	in	the direction	of lowertariffs. When I look at this particular bill I	wonder why	we	have not adopted the
method outlined in article XVI, as amended, of the general agreement on tariffs and trade, to which the hon. member for Greenwood referred as GATT, as it is popularly known.
I should just like to indicate what I mean. I	have before	me	the protocol	and the
amendment to article XVI of the agreement on tariffs and trade. Perhaps it will suffice if I just give the amendment. It states:
Article XVI shall be amended as follows:
. . . The following new section shall be added:
"Section B-Additional Provisions on Export Subsidies"
"2. The contracting parties recognize that the granting by a contracting party of a subsidy on the export of any product may have harmful effects for other contracting parties, both importing and exporting, may cause undue disturbance to their normal commercial interests, and may hinder the achievement of the objectives of this agreement.
"3. Accordingly, contracting parties should seek to avoid the use of subsidies on the export of primary products. If, however, a contracting party grants directly or indirectly any form of subsidy which operates to increase the export of any primary product from its territory, such subsidy shall not be applied in a manner which results in that contracting party having more than an equitable share of world export trade in that product, account being taken of the shares of the contracting parties in such trade in the product during a previous representative period, and any special factors which may have affected or may be affecting such trade in the product.
It goes on to say:
Contracting parties shall notify the contracting parties . . .
And so on. Then it says:
(c) The contracting parties may, at the request of a contracting party which has reason to believe that its interests under this agreement are being adversely affected by the operations of an enterprise of the kind described in paragraph 1 (a), request the contracting party establishing, maintaining or authorizing such enterprise to supply information about its operation related to the carrying out of the provisions of this agreement.
Customs Tariff
(d) The provisions of this paragraph shall not require any contracting party to disclose confidential information which would impede law enforcement or otherwise be contrary to the public interest or would prejudice the legitimate commercial interests of particular enterprises.
It seems to me that instead of enacting the clause which we have in the bill at the present time, we should follow the method outlined in GATT and should exhaust all the possibilities of GATT before we approve the kind of power which is given to the governor in council in this bill. Of course we also have the dumping act which can be used in addition to anything the governor in council may authorize.
That dumping act itself, it seems to me, has been used in a manner which would discourage the importation of subsidized goods. I notice a short time ago that the Minister of National Revenue-of course I cannot quote exactly what he said-told us that as the result of Bill No. 29 there was a deterrent effect upon importers of certain lines of goods into Canada, because they did not know just what the value would be and what their bill would be for duty purposes.
It seems to me that is a wrong principle. If we are operating under the rule of law, then the House of Commons should lay down what the duty should be and should not leave it to the ministry, or more particularly should not leave it to the guesswork of the importer. He should have some assurance of what conditions he will be required to fulfil in order to import goods into this country. It seems to me that this particular clause of this particular bill, or the part of it to which I have referred, and the dumping act together may be a potent and effective weapon in our tariff and trade policy.
I think we were moving in the right direction when we were reducing the barriers against trade into this country. After all, the goods that flow into this country are in payment of the goods we export. The higher we build the wall, or the more difficulties we put in the way of importers bringing goods into this country, the more difficult it is for us to sell goods.
Looking at this bill, I greatly regret clause 1 which, it seems to me, does something that we should not do. It gives the governor in council more power over the decision as to what tariffs shall be levied against goods coming from a country in which subsidization has been resorted to. It seems to me that the GATT agreement calling for consultation is the method we should use.
Over the last several days we have heard a great deal about the granting of powers to the Minister of Defence Production, and

Customs Tariff
we have heard a great deal of criticism of those powers. I want to say that in clause 1 of this bill I consider power is given as great as or greater than that given to the Minister of Defence Production; not only is that power given, but it is given in a field which I think is indefensible.
I am not going to deal with the defence production bill at the moment. I shall have something to say about it when it comes before the house again. Perhaps I can say this at the moment. I can see the necessity for that particular bill at the present time. But it seems to me that this bill is far more important, because it deals with goods that are imported into this country for the use of Canadians and it gives to the governor in council, in addition to the dumping act, powers which create uncertainty in the minds of importers and which may have the effect, if the government and the minister so desire, of preventing goods from coming into this country and of placing upon them not only a higher tariff but indeed, in some instances, perhaps an effective embargo.
When I look at the schedules-and I shall not deal with that matter; one of my colleagues will do so-I find that you have there a duty placed on a commodity which the Canadian people find to be essential in the colder winter months of the year. I therefore want to protest against this bill because I think it violates the rule of law and I think it violates the responsibilities of this parliament, which should decide what tariffs are to be levied against goods. We are placing in the hands of the ministry a power which, in consideration of the immense power contained in the anti-dumping act which we have on the statute books, in my opinion threatens the whole of our trade policy, if we do not make an effective protest at this time.

Mr. Speaker, there is just one brief remark I should like to make. It is in the same sense as that in which I spoke on June 21, as reported at page 5116 of Hansard. I am moved to make this remark by the presence in the house on this occasion of the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver), who was not in the house at the moment when I spoke on June 21.
Having regard to what he had to say on May 30, as reported at page 4261 of Hansard, and to the errors he then made in his reference to the trade policies of the parties represented here I should like to draw to his attention, as I did to that of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) and any other advocates of free trade under the banners of
the Liberal party, the fact that this is a
government measure, one of the effects of which is to introduce increases in the tariff; and that in supporting the bill, as presumably they are, they are giving support to increases in the tariff.

On clause 3-Schedule A further amended.

Clause 3 of the bill refers to certain tariff items which appear in schedule B, and which are to become part of schedule A to the act, if it is passed. I would refer particularly to item 207c which refers to ethylene glycol and mixtures of ethylene glycol and other glycols in which ethylene glycol predominates, for use in the manufacture of antifreezing compounds. In the rate schedule there is shown a proposed British preferential tariff of 10 per cent, a most favoured nation tariff of 10 per cent, and a general tariff of 25 per cent.
When we were on the budget resolutions a few days ago I raised this question with the Minister of Finance and inquired why he proposed to place tariffs of 10 per cent and 25 per cent on an article or commodity which hitherto has had free entry. As I understand it, if it has been imported for the purpose of making explosives it has been on the free list since 1926. Since 1939 it has been on the free list for both antifreeze and explosive purposes. It is proposed to leave the ethylene glycol to be used in the manufacture of explosives on the free list, but to impose tariffs of 10 per cent and 25 per cent on the glycol used in the manufacture of antifreeze.
When I inquired of the minister as to the reasons for that, he expressed the preference that this question should be left until the bill was before the house. In order to accommodate the minister I did that. Now that the bill is before the house it is important that we give due consideration to this rather major change.
It is a major change in two respects, Mr. Chairman. In the first place it involves a commodity which is very widely used in Canada, particularly in the agricultural parts of Canada and perhaps more particularly on the prairie provinces, where antifreeze is a commodity that is used not only for domestic purposes by those who own automobiles and so forth but is also used in tractors, combines, trucks and all other vehicles that have to be

Customs Tariff
exposed to below freezing temperatures. It is easy to imagine the great effect it might have on the price of antifreeze if this protection gives the Canadian manufacturers of antifreeze, or of the base product, ethylene glycol, an opportunity to raise their prices unduly.
I have gone over the tariff board hearings on this question, as suggested by the minister, and I am not too sure that we come to the same conclusions. Quite obviously we do not, because I am opposed to the imposition of this tariff. Apparently the minister is in favour of it. On going through the hearings before the tariff board we learn that there were originally two companies that made representations calling for the imposition of a tariff. Up until November, 1954, the two companies interested were the Dow Chemical Company of Canada and the Dominion Tar and Chemical Company of Canada. There was a slight change in the line-up in November of 1954, because Union Carbide Canada, which is a subsidiary of Union Carbide of the United States, purchased the plant owned by the Dominion Tar and Chemical Company in Montreal East, and then of course became directly interested in this product.
What is the result? Representations were made actually by three companies, but as a matter of fact there are only two companies now which are in a position to manufacture ethylene glycol in Canada. In addition to that, I am given to understand that Dow Chemical itself is a subsidiary of a United States company, which is Dow Chemical of Midland, U.S.A. So here we have the situation that at the present time two companies, both subsidiaries of parent companies in the United States, appear before the Canadian tariff board to argue for the imposition of a tariff on the base used in the making of antifreeze.
What are they asking? I turn to the evidence again, and I should like to read from the words of their own representative to show what they are actually doing. On page 55 of the evidence of October 5, 1954, Mr. W. T. Wood, who appeared for Dow Chemical Company of Canada, is reported as having given the following evidence. The chairman asked him the following question with reference to the brief which had already been presented:
I see these words "rightful share of the domestic market". If your cost is 17 cents (that is per pound) and the United States is 10 cents, and the tariff were such as to bring the laid down cost of the American product to 17 cents then you would have the entire market.
The entire market, which the present Canadian manufacturer almost requires.

So, your meaning of "rightful
share" is the whole market?

Yes.
That is clear enough and categorical enough. What those companies are asking is that the imposition of the tariff shall have the effect of handing over to them, both now subsidiaries of parent companies in the United States, the whole Canadian market for ethylene glycol. That to me is a dangerous situation, because when we consider the possibilities of what two big manufacturing outfits of that nature can do, to combine and set up a virtual monopoly in that field and then push up the price of their product to suit themselves, we can see that it certainly would not be in the public interest to take the step which is being proposed.
What about prices? Nowhere in the evidence was I able to find that either of these companies that asked for virtually the whole Canadian market for ethylene glycol presented its balance sheet or statement of profit and loss. At one point there was some question asked as to the financial position of one of the companies, and they declined to answer. Of course it is their own business if they wish to keep their balance sheet confidential. I am not going to argue about that so far as the tariff board hearings were concerned. But certainly when the government proposes an increase in the tariff item dealing with ethylene glycol for the benefit of two companies that are out to get the whole Canadian market, according to the statement of their own representative, then I think we have the right to demand and have the balance sheets of these companies laid before us in order that we might know just what financial position they are in, and whether they are justified in asking for this protection.
As to the retail prices of antifreeze, there is quite a range. I am going to give the figures that were presented by the tariff board itself as the result of a survey that was made in 42 centres in Canada in 1954, as presented in their report. They found that the retail prices ranged from $3.95 to $4.25 a gallon. On going through the evidence further I found that the manufactured cost of ethylene glycol in Canada in 1954 ranged from $1.45 to $1.65 a gallon. That is the same product that, when mixed with a few detergents and other chemicals to turn it into antifreeze, retails at from $3.95 to $4.25 a gallon. That is a tremendous spread, and in itself would indicate that these companies are in a position to make a pretty hefty profit.
I should like to refer to some of the evidence of the representative of Radio Oil Refineries, who have a plant in Winnipeg

and who are in the business of what they describe as canning the antifreeze; that is, they buy the base product and put it through whatever process is necessary and put it into cans for the wholesale trade. They put it through whatever process is necessary in order to prepare it for the wholesale trade. Mr. Hechter, who represented Radio Oil Refineries Limited, was reported on page 74 of the submission as saying:
Today, when you have only two companies in Canada which manufacture ethylene glycol, if you put a tariff on, you set up a monopoly.
That is pretty strong language from one who is so intimately connected with the trade and who I think would be in position to know.
Whether you like it or not that is actually what is happening.
Then on the next page of the submission:
Ethylene glycol brought into this country has to be treated and handled before it is fit for automotive use. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I am personally very much opposed to the restriction of free enterprise by placing this tariff on and if you place this tariff on you are going to jeopardize us in western Canada by giving us a higher cost.
That is a categorical statement which sets out the opinion of the representative of that company. Of course I have not dealt with all the evidence, in the interests of brevity and in an effort not to hold up the work of this committee. But I submit it indicates that there is a good reason why this committee should be very cautious about allowing this item to slip through at this time. The government has not attempted to make a case for the imposition of a tariff on ethylene glycol, and the companies which appeared before the tariff board certainly made out no case so far as their financial position was concerned.
It is reported that Union Carbide paid in the neighbourhood of $5 million for the plant of Dominion Tar in November, 1954, which would indicate that in making an investment of that size at that time they must have expected to be successful in selling their product. It certainly would not indicate that the market situation was such that these companies were suffering from undue competition from the United States.
As I said, the companies did not make out a case which was satisfactory to me or to anyone who is interested in the consumer of this product. So far the government has made out no case. The statements of the representatives of these companies make it quite clear that the motive or objective is to corner the Canadian market. Under those circumstances I would suggest that we would be wise to leave ethylene glycol on the free list as before.
Customs Tariff
If the companies which have made this request will supply us with details of their financial position in an effort to show that they require protection in the future, then the matter can be brought before the house again. But on the face of the evidence given at the tariff board hearing and on the face of a situation where the two major companies in Canada are in position to form a virtual monopoly and restrict competition, I should think we would be well advised not to accept the proposal of the government. That is one ground on which this is a major change of policy.
Before I go on to deal with the other matter I have in mind I should like to mention that the tariff board report was not unanimous. Apparently one member of the board, I believe it was Mr. Leduc, submitted a minority report in which he opposed any change in the tariff items covering ethylene glycol and antifreeze. He stated his reasons for so doing, and that is an additional reason why the members of this committee should not at this time accept the proposal of the government. If one of the members of the tariff board who heard all the evidence given at all the meetings was not convinced as to the wisdom of this move, then certainly the members of this committee should hesitate before-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: He was in favour of the increase; it was the decrease in antifreeze there was some dissent about.

The gentleman who put in
the minority report stated that he was not in favour of any change in the tariff items which would remove ethylene glycol from the free list.
The other matter to which I wanted to refer as a major change of policy is the noticeable trend, to which my leader referred earlier, on the part of this government to-become more and more protectionist, to become a high-tariff government. I say that with a certain amount of sadness rather than anger, because there are many people on the prairies who over the years have been persuaded that the Liberal party is the low-tariff party of Canada. I can remember attending meetings where I heard politicians holding forth on the question of high tariffs or low tariffs. In those days it was quite clear that the Liberals and the Progressives, who later became the Liberal Progressives, were the advocates of free trade or the closest thing possible to free trade; were in favour of removing all restrictions, customs tariffs and so on, and then on the other side were the Conservatives, who were holding out for higher tariffs and greater protection.

Customs Tariff
A sort of pattern or mould was established in western Canada, and I think the government will admit that there was no question as to which political philosophy the people of the prairie provinces favoured. For example, when the Progressive party came out as a strong free trade party, one of the strongest we have ever had since the early days of the Liberal party, they swept the prairie provinces and their representatives in this house did a grand job in trying to remove as many restrictions as possible to international trade. But as time went on and others came along that was brushed aside or forgotten, but there still lingered in the minds of the people out west the belief that the Liberal party was the low-tariff party and the Conservative party the high-tariff party.
That this no longer is the case is quite unmistakable. Going back to 1953 we had Bill No. 29, which was the foot in the door, the thin edge of the wedge. That bill placed the Minister of National Revenue in the position of being able to virtually dictate what the customs duty shall be on particular items attempting to enter Canada. We have had it in his own words that that bill was instrumental in raising the duty on certain items that entered Canada and had prevented perhaps an indefinite volume of goods from entering this country because those who wished to export to Canada, particularly from the United States, could not know just what the duty would be. That uncertainty prevented them from attempting to send their goods into Canada. I hope I am correctly interpreting what the minister said.
As time went on we had another bill passed in the course of this session which gave the Minister of National Revenue some extra power along the same lines. Now we have this tariff item which places an impost upon a commodity which is very widely used across Canada, particularly in the west.
The thing that bothers me is this. Much as I disagree with the philosophy with respect to tariffs of my friends of the Progressive Conservative party, I must admit that I have a little more admiration for the way they go about it than I have at the present time for the Liberal party. I say that not in a spirit of bitterness, but in a spirit of sadness. At least the Conservative members make it clear that they believe in higher tariffs and they have no objection to big business getting bigger and better protection.
That is fine. Even big business is entitled to representation in this house. In a democracy everyone is entitled to be represented. Anyway, they state their case. As I say, I disagree with it most heartily. But what is the policy now of the Liberal party? They

do not come out and say to us, "We have decided to become as conservative as the Conservatives have become progressive. We are now going to take a certain part of the Conservative policy and put it into our statutes by raising the tariffs on seven items, and we are going to stand by it." They sneak these tariff increases in through side doors, through the back door, through the chimney and everywhere except through the front door, with the exception of the one we are now discussing, which gives us an opportunity to face the situation.
For example, clause 1 of this bill, which gives the Minister of National Revenue almost indefinite and infinite discretion, is merely a back-door method-I was going to say a sneaky method, but I do not like to use that word, though perhaps it would be more explicit-of doing the same thing which they have denounced the Conservatives for attempting to do in the last two or three days.
It is time the people of this country knew what was going on and came to the realization that, so far as the party which supports the government is concerned, it is no longer the low-tariff party. Any resemblance between liberalism and the present Liberal party is purely coincidental. It has become a restric-tionist, protectionist, high-tariff outfit and is doing the same things it has denounced the Conservatives for doing, but it is doing them chiefly through the back-door method. However, in this item they are doing it openly.
I say these things because a great deal more than tariffs is involved. What happens when we allow this government to increase the restrictions on imports? They benefit huge industrial concerns like the two to which I have referred, which are in a perfect position to form a combine and monopolize the whole field, and even have the temerity to state before the tariff board that this is their objective. If the government are doing that in order to assist them to corner the market, they are being the handmaidens of monopoly in this country.
That is also a trend which is causing many of us concern. Not long ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce played his part in the setting up of a pipe-line combine, which has been his problem child ever since. Now we have the government assisting in the setting up of an antifreeze combine which, if predictions work out, is going to result in a much higher cost of antifreeze to the consumer in Canada.
On the basis of all these things it is time the private members of this house-and not only those on this side of the house-protested. As a matter of fact I do not expect

much support on this from my Progressive Conservative friends, because I think they are in favour of this tariff. I sensed that; but I shall leave that to them. Certainly my friends to the left, of the Social Credit party, and about 50 per cent of my Liberal friends across the way should be on their feet fighting this instead of sitting back and letting the government assist two big companies, both subsidiaries of companies in the United States, to corner the Canadian market for this commodity and bring the price up to suit themselves.
I should like to hear some of these free traders from the prairies raise their voices. I should like to hear a storm of protest before this session ends, so that for once the private members of this house, regardless of where they sit, will tell the government what they think of its tariff policy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I
reply at once to the hon. member for Dauphin? He has informed the committee that he has read the tariff board report in which these three tariff item changes have been recommended. I am surprised, however, that having read it, he could so badly misread it and particularly misinterpret it to the house. I believe he has the document in his hand, and I ask him again to read the minority report to which he referred.
I would point out to him that the board was unanimous in the matter of recommending a flat 10 per cent on the ethylene glycol in both the pure and the impure type. The board split two to one in favour of the reduction from 20 per cent to 15 per cent on the antifreeze the finished product the consumer uses, which this government has implemented in item 207d. The antifreeze compounds, with which his constituents would be chiefly familiar, were reduced from 20 per cent to 15 per cent.
I would emphasize to the house that there is no net increase of protection in this field. There is merely a rearrangement of a group of rates that previously were rather unbalanced. The tariff board so recommended. This statement can most clearly be substantiated by the fact that these were items that were covered by a GATT agreement.
Hon. members will recognize that the chief contracting party affected in the most favoured nation group would, of course, be the United States. In order to make a readjustment of this item, following the tariff board report, it was necessary to approach the United States and do some negotiating. The United States was prepared to make a trade, under which they accepted an increase in item 207c from the rate of free and 20 per cent to 10 per cent in return for the
