speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the gist of the motion that is now under discussion with the amendment is that the government should give consideration to instituting the necessary consultation and inquiry in respect to reform of the Senate, so that appropriate steps may be taken, including such matters as the method by which members of the Senate shall be chosen, so the Senate may more effectively discharge
fThe Chairman.]

the constitutional function it was intended to perform as an integral part of our parliamentary system.
This question is not new. From time to time the question of so-called Senate reform has been the topic of discussion not only on the platforms of political parties but in the press of this country. References to debates in parliament going back a good many years have already been made by previous speakers in this debate.
I was interested to note the reprint of a quotation from an editorial that appeared in the Eastern Chronicle of February 17, 1895, about 60 years ago. It said:
There are now 11 vacancies in the Senate, and during the approaching election they will be used to demonstrate the utility from a ministerial standpoint of that effete institution. The promise of an annuity of $1,000 with prestige is most seductive. In fact, it has a cash value. Truly Canadians are a good natured people.
So even back 60 years ago the upper chamber of this parliament was the subject of criticism. But more important, the manner in which vacancies in that chamber were filled or left vacant was under severe criticism.
I think it is important that we should look into this question carefully. If we take a superficial view of it we may say that the upper chamber of this parliament has lost the confidence of the Canadian people, or that the confidence of the people in that chamber is beginning to waver, and that therefore the thing to do is to do away with it. I feel that people who come to that conclusion-a rather shallow one, I suggest-do so for the wrong reason. It is true that at the present time the Senate is ineffective, and that in most cases it is more or less a rubber stamp for government legislation passing through this chamber. But to say that does not mean the institution itself is bad. It has become ineffective because of the method by which its membership has been appointed. And to say that the Senate is ineffective at the present time and therefore it should be done away with, is similar to the reasoning of the man who refused to jump out of the thirteenth story window of a building because he was superstitious.
One must realize that although at the present time the Senate is not fulfilling to the greatest extent the functions for which it was intended, the institution in itself is a good one; and I believe it is a good one, for various reasons. The most important of these reasons is that it is a body whose membership has greater security in office than those in the elected chamber. They can vote against legislation if they think it is in the public interest to do so, even if that legislation has

a passing and transient popularity. Due to the greater stability in office of the membership of that body they do not have to fear reprisals from the electorate at a following election because they turned something down that might have looked good until it was brought into effect and proven bad.
So the Senate is a chamber which, if properly constituted, can take a sober second look at legislation passed by the lower house. In that way it has an inhibiting effect on the lower chamber, if the membership of that chamber should contemplate legislation which would be popular with the electorate for a short period of time, but which those in the lower house may know in their hearts would not be sound or for the good of the country.
Most of our provinces do not have an upper chamber, and most of the colonies, before they joined confederation, had no upper chambers. It is argued by some, and there is justification for the argument, that had Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland had upper chambers in their legislatures they might not have become the victims of governments which, in their efforts to spend money on projects which were in popular demand, put their colonies in debt to a greater extent than they could afford, with the result that those colonies felt compelled to join confederation.
Then, too, in most cases an upper chamber gives an opportunity for various minorities to have stable representation in parliament. There is representation for racial and vocational groups, and representation by various parties, when such a system functions properly. Most important of all is the fact that regional areas have proper representation in parliament. Representation in most lower [DOT]chambers of parliament is roughly by population. In most countries it is recognized, however, that population as such is not the only thing that requires representation in parliament. Areas and natural resources must be represented, and we find recognition of that fact in this House of Commons. Here we have members representing large but sparsely populated areas, and we think immediately [DOT]of constituencies such as Mackenzie River and Yukon. On the other hand we have examples of isolated areas which have representation in the House of Commons although their population does not justify it. And in that category I think of the constituency of Iles-de-la-Madeleine.
In many dominions, such as Australia and New Zealand, that principle is recognized in a regular formula which sets out the unit of representation in rural areas as being smaller than that in urban districts. I think it was the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) who made the
Proposed Senate Reform observation that he did not think it was reasonable that his province should have only six senators while New Brunswick, with a much smaller population, has ten.
I would point out that the very purpose behind the way in which representation in the Senate was established was that the various colonies which formed the Dominion of Canada in the first instance should be represented in the parliament of Canada. And so their voices would not be submerged to the point where their weight would be almost negligible, the representation was not made strictly on the basis of population. They were independent, but agreed to come into confederation provided they would always continue to have a reasonable voice in the parliament of Canada. On that understanding the maritime provinces were given 24 seats in the Senate; Quebec, 24; Ontario, 24; and the four western provinces between them, 24 more. The number of senators in relation to the population varies greatly, of course. As a matter of fact, in Prince Edward Island there is a senator for every 23,000 people while in Ontario, the other extreme, there is one senator for every 158,000 people.
But I point out that that state of affairs is intentional and exists in practically every upper chamber of every parliament or congress in the world. In the United States, for instance, although their Senate is elected, each state has the right to elect two senators. The smallest state by way of population, namely Nevada, with a population of only 160,000, elects two senators to the United States Senate; while New York, with a population of over 15 million, elects only two senators.
The purpose of that provision, of course, is that these regional districts or states which came into the union shall continue to have a voice which counts in the parliament of the country as a whole. The same is true in Australia. In that country each state elects 10 senators. The population of the Australian states varies from Western Australia with a population of roughly 600,000 to New South Wales with a population of 3,500,000, yet they have the same number of senators.
There is another important factor as far as membership in the Senate is concerned. At the present time this chiefly concerns the maritime provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. When the various colonies came into confederation it was agreed, as I have already said, that they should have a certain fixed number of seats in the Senate. It was also agreed that they should have a certain number of seats in the House of Commons at the beginning. The
5482	HOUSE OF
Proposed Senate Reform province of British Columbia had an agreement firmly laid down that it would be represented by six members in the House of Commons, and that its representation in the House of Commons would never fall below six members, regardless of what its population might be. The provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island were under the delusion that their agreement was of the same kind.
When Prince Edward Island went into confederation in 1873 it was granted four seats in the Senate and six in the House of Commons, and the islanders were under the impression that their membership in the House of Commons would never fall below six. They were rather amazed to find that after the redistribution of 1892 their membership was cut from six to five, and in 1904 from five to four. After the census of 1911 it became evident that their membership in the House of Commons would be cut from four to three if the trend were allowed to continue. The matter was taken to the courts, but after a great deal of litigation the provinces of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, which tried to establish their right to the original number of seats in the House of Commons, failed to do so both before the Supreme Court of Canada and the privy council.
I think that was around 1904. They employed as their counsel on that occasion Sir Allen Aylesworth. The two provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island lost their case. However, in 1905, the following year, Sir Allen Aylesworth became the minister of justice and my province and New Brunswick thought their chance had come, that they were in luck. It was with great chagrin they learned that after their counsel was firmly established as minister of justice he war. dead against the principle of allowing the original number of seats in the House of Commons for those two provinces.
At a later time, after the Borden government had come to office, the British North America Act was amended so the membership of any province in the House of Commons would never fall below its representation in the Senate. In other words the membership in the Senate was to be the floor for representation in the Commons. At the present time Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick are protected by that floor. They also, of course, went on the assumption, when they came into confederation, that one of the terms of the agreement was that they should have a certain number of seats in the Senate. They assumed that those seats would be filled, that they would not remain vacant for long periods of time.


I think this government has neglected its moral responsibility in this regard, and has even neglected its legal responsibility. Section 32 of the British North America Act reads:
When a vacancy happens in the Senate by resignation, death, or otherwise, the governor general shall by summons to a fit and qualified person fill the vacancy.
I would take that to mean that the vacancy should be filled within a reasonable time. I think it is fair to say that this government has repudiated not only its moral obligations in this regard but its legal obligations as well, by leaving a large number of seats in the Senate vacant for long periods of time. As of last December there were 20 vacancies in the Senate. This is a means of sabotaging that chamber.
I have no criticism of the membership of that house as individuals. I think the institution as such is a good and necessary one; but if seats are left vacant for long periods of time, or filled only by men whose prime requisite for membership in that body is that they are unquestioning supporters of the government in power, then it is not good enough. When things are carried on in that way the Senate is bound to be frustrated and rendered almost non-effective.
Some say, of course, that as far as the protection of representation of smaller provinces in the Commons is concerned, arrangements could be made to take care of that, and the simple thing to do is wipe out the Senate and do away with it. I think that is a most superficial way of looking at the matter; I believe that is something at which we should have a second look.
As far as I can learn, almost without exception those countries which have drawn up new constitutions in recent years have provided for upper houses. No doubt they have drawn on their previous experience and felt there was a necessity for upper houses. I have looked up the action taken recently by a number of these countries when they adopted new constitutions. I find that the Irish Free State introduced its new constitution in 1937, and it has a senate. Iceland introduced a new constitution in 1944, and it has a senate. France introduced a new constitution in 1946, and it has a senate. Ceylon and India took this action in 1947, and both have upper houses. West Germany did the same in 1949, and it has a senate.
In fairness I must say that most of the countries in the democratic world have senates. Most South American countries have senates patterned on that of the United States, and the same is true of Australia-

However, there are exceptions. New Zealand abolished its upper chamber in 1950, but that is the only country that has done so in recent years. Denmark has no upper chamber; but it is interesting to note that when Iceland, which is so closely related to Denmark in many ways, introduced a new constitution recently they provided for a senate. I know it can be argued with a great deal of validity that there is justification for a second chamber in this and any other parliament provided it is properly constituted.
That brings us to the methods by which vacancies in a senate should be filled or how that body should be constituted. The Senate of the United States is elected by popular vote but the representation is not according to population; it is by area, as I have pointed out already. The same system obtains in most South American countries, and also in Australia.
In Ireland there is a senate with a membership of 60, 11 of whom are appointed by the president, 3 of whom are elected by the national university, 3 by the University of Dublin, and the remaining 43 are elected from a slate of candidates who in the first place are selected according to vocation in order that labour and the professions will have representation in the senate.
In South Africa some of the membership is appointed by the government but the majority of the membership is elected by the provincial legislature and the members of parliament from that province meeting together and electing the representatives of that province to the senate. In most cases where senates are elected the term of office is longer than that of the lower house, or they are elected a third at a time, or the election takes place at a time which does not coincide with the election for the lower chamber. This is done to give a certain continuity to the parliament of the country.
In Switzerland the senate is elected by the provinces, and the same is true of France and Germany. In the case of France the election is by the various departments, and in the case of West Germany it is by the Lander. The same or a very similar system obtains in Belgium. In the case of the Netherlands the provinces elect their representatives to the upper house. In the case of Sweden the election is by popular vote but the term is twice as long as that for the lower chamber, eight years as compared with four.
In Norway they have a most interesting method of constituting their upper house, and I would be most intrigued with the impact of such a method upon this chamber. There the parliament is elected by popular vote, and
Proposed Senate Reform at the first meeting of parliament the members elect 25 per cent of their membership to constitute the upper house.
Do they sit in both houses?

No, they sit in only one. Depending upon their point of view, the representatives can elect a man who is popular and highly qualified to the upper house or, on the other hand, I imagine if there was someone who was objectionable they could banish him to the upper house.
I think it is agreed by almost all democratic countries that an upper house can fill a most useful purpose. I agree with that point of view and I think most Canadians will agree with it. But in order that a senate may fulfil the functions for which it is intended, its membership must be selected in some reasonable and workable fashion. I think it is most important that large numbers of seats in the Senate should not be left vacant for long periods of time. As I have said already, I think this government is abdicating its responsibility when it leave seats in the upper chamber vacant for long periods of time.
This creates the impression in the public mind that the Senate is something that does not matter, that the seats there are simply plums to be handed out to followers of the party in power, to people who have consistently followed the party line. If the Senate of Canada is to regain the confidence the Canadian people should have in it, it is essential that vacancies be filled immediately. Also, as this motion says, consideration should be given to the best method of selecting or electing the members required to fill these vacancies. I feel that this government owes it to our country and to our parliamentary institutions to take steps to reform the Senate-and when I say that I mean the method of constituting the Senate-at the earliest possible time.

Mr. Speaker, following the speech of the hon. member who has just spoken, it seems to me that quite a number of things I wanted to say have already been said. However, I am going to be brief, and I am going to remember what you, Mr. Speaker, admonished me about when in the fall of 1953 I rose in this house to say something on this same subject. You said I was to be more careful in how I referred to the upper chamber and its membership.
Over the years since then a great number of editorials have appeared in the press across Canada speculating as to what should, could and might be done as far as the reform of the Senate was concerned. I am going

Proposed Senate Reform to use only part of an editorial that appeared in the Ottawa Journal on the 2nd of June, 1954. I shall read two paragraphs:
And, alter all, what Is it that is wrong with the Senate at this time? All that is wrong-unless we agree that the parliament set up by the B.N.A. Act is not something we want any more-is that the government has been treating the Senate, treating a part of parliament, with disdain, if not contempt.
It goes on to say:
Nor is it a question of the government setting out to appoint Conservatives to the Senate, to redress its existing pitifully lopsided party standing. Such a step would help for the time being at any rate; but the real need is for appointments of men, whether Liberal, Conservative, Social Credit, C.C.F. or of no party at all, who would compel the confidence of the country and know what our constitution, our form of government, and the functions of the Senate are about.
That points out some of the problems the government of today must be facing. I am safe in saying also, from my contact with my own constituents and from these editorials in the newspapers, that the prestige of the upper house at the present time is at an alltime low.
When I mention that and mention Senate reform, I do not suppose any man's name comes to mind more frequently than does that of the late prime minister, Right Hon. Mackenzie King. He used that as a theme through many years, and fairly effectively. The pages of Hansard record Mr. King's speeches fairly liberally, and they are interspersed with promises of reform of the upper chamber from time to time. It would be advisable now if the government of the day were to read, mark and inwardly digest some of the speeches he made through the years when he was in opposition. Having done so, they could then probably arrange a seance with the spirit to try to discover what changes, if any, might be suggested. I am certain that if such a seance were arranged the answer would come back, "Yes, make some changes".
I took the trouble to look up some of the purposes for which the upper house was created. First and foremost, it was to protect the rights of minorities. I ask the present members of the cabinet, how often in the past 10 years has the upper chamber fulfilled that purpose? As far as I can recall, not once in the past 10 years has it tried in any way to protect the rights of minorities.
The second purpose I wish to mention was to protect the rights of individuals, and to protect the people of Canada from radical legislation. If there is one item of radical legislation before us at the present time, it is the question of defence production. I wonder what the upper house might do with that?

speechtext: May I interrupt the hon. member just to ask him to be careful, not only when he analyses the past conduct of the hon. members of the other house but when he tries to forecast what they will do in the future. Very good, Mr. Speaker. I think it was an old lady who said, if you could not speak well of the devil, you could at least say he was a busy individual.
The upper chamber was constituted to unite upper and lower Canada; to protect both upper and lower Canada as to their race, religion and language; to maintain a balance as between the maritimes, central and western Canada; to avert and avoid the difficulties the United States of America were experiencing at the very time of confederation, the differences between the north and the south and the weaknesses of the constitution that were evident at that time; and to provide strong safeguards for provincial and sectional interests.
At this point I wish to quote from Mac-Kay's "The Unreformed Senate of Canada". On page 37 Mr. MacKay points out what Sir John A. Macdonald had to say on the second day of the Quebec conference:
The essential features of the proposed upper house were outlined by John A. Macdonald on the second day of the conference.
"Now as to the constitution of the legislature we should have two chambers, an upper and a lower house. In the upper house equality in numbers should be the basis, in the lower house population should be the basis. . . . The mode of appointment to the upper house-Many are in favour of election and many are in favour of appointment by the crown ... I am after experience in both systems in favour of returning to the old system of nomination by the crown ..."
At that time they were pointing out the basis of representation that my colleague so well described a few minutes ago. Other countries have abolished the second chamber. Back in 1953 I suggested that if some constructive action were not taken the demand for abolition would become more vociferous and insistent. That is actually what has

happened, with a greater degree of insistence during the last couple of years. It has become an actual fact.
I need only refer again to these editorials. Back on November 24, 1953, I had this to say; and so far, from editorials that I have read and the statement of the Prime Minister on one occasion, I have not had any reason to change my mind or what I had to say on that date. I am just going to read two paragraphs of what I said on that occasion. It is to be found on page 275 of Hansard for 1953-54:
I am going to suggest, sir, that at no time should the opposition in the other house be lower than 25 per cent of the total membership and that at least one-third and preferably one-half of the members should be appointed by the provincial governments in power-the numbers being in direct relation to the population of the area entitled to representation under the constitution. I suggest that all appointments be for a term not to exceed ten years, or until age 75, whichever shall occur first. If this suggestion were followed, the rise and fall of the fortunes of political parties in the provinces and in the dominion would be reflected in the membership of that chamber.
The government now has a mandate from the people for at least four years before there will be another general election. There will be abundant time in which to give this matter some serious thought, and to introduce the amendments required.
I therefore ask the Prime Minister and his government to give serious consideration to the plan roughly outlined in order to restore the confidence of the Canadian people in the other place, to ensure to minority groups that their rights will be protected, and to ensure to all individuals the most cherished right under democratic government, namely, the freedom of the individual.

Mr. Speaker, from the tone of the debate thus far I think we can conclude that most hon. members would agree that the second chamber has become an integral part of our parliamentary system. In fact the only dissenting opinion in the chamber seems to be that of the C.C.F. group, who would rather lean in the direction of abolition.
As I have studied this problem over the past few years, I have never found much support for the abolitionist viewpoint. I remember that back in 1952 the Manitoba Tuxis boys' parliament came out strongly for abolition, but I do not think we can take that as a responsible position. However, notwithstanding the fact that we agree on the principle of bicameralism, there always is agitation in this chamber and in the press across the country for reform of the Senate. Therefore, for the first time I want to say just a few words on this important matter.
I believe the whole problem boils down to one major difficulty. That difficulty is the tendency for the upper chamber to take on a lop-sided partisan appearance. This situation, of course, results from the fact that 50433-346
Proposed Senate Reform appointments to the Senate are gifts of the party in power; and down through the years since confederation the Senate has tended to become dominated by the partisan supporters of the particular party in power.
The reason the Senate is basic in Canada has been outlined already by many members in this discussion. The authorities tell us that had it not been for the device of the second chamber, in all probability confederation could not have been achieved. At this point I should just like to suggest that perhaps the function of the second chamber in protecting the rights of the provinces and other minorities is not as important today as it was when Canada first became a nation.
That is mainly because we have other devices for dealing with problems that arise in different provinces. For example, we now use to an increasing extent the device or the machinery of the dominion-provincial conference. By that means, rather than by the action of the Senate, we try to resolve the differences of opinion on various subjects that occur from time to time among the various provinces making up the Dominion of Canada. We must also remember that the Supreme Court of Canada is now the last court of appeal. That fact, to a certain extent, has decreased the function of the Senate of taking care of provincial and minority rights.
Notwithstanding those changes, Mr. Speaker, I feel that the Senate, as I said at the outset of my remarks, is still an integral part of our parliamentary system and that it will continue to be so if this house-and particularly the government-has sufficient vision and energy to carry out the reforms necessary to make the Senate operate efficiently in the changed conditions that surround us today.
More recently the government has been very quiet on the matter of Senate reform. In fact, as I read back through the pages of Hansard covering this debate, I find that we have had only one representative from the government side take any part in the discussion of this important subject. I recall that a few years ago the topic of Senate reform was a lively one in Liberal circles, particularly at election time. Perhaps the reason we no longer hear of this particular issue today is that the government has become so strong in Canada that it hardly needs any election platform any more. As someone has said, so strong is its influence and so thorough is the grip of its various propaganda outlets on the people of Canada that it could win an election on a laundry ticket or on no ticket at all.

Proposed Senate Reform
With the trend toward a one-party state which has been evident in the country, particularly in the years since the war, I feel that the function of the Senate is even more important today than it ever was, particularly the adequate functioning of a reformed Senate. With the trend toward a powerful one-party government there is the tendency toward increasing control on the part of the executive arm of government. That tendency has been evident in recent days in the thrust for power made by one particular member of the cabinet. This danger was seen in Canada by statesmen long before the actual process became obvious.
I should like to quote the words of an outstanding Liberal member of this house from western Canada, who foresaw in very precise terms just the situation that faces the parliament of Canada today. These are the words of Sir Clifford Sifton:
No nation should be under unchecked, singlechamber government. According to my experience, the will of the people is very often better expressed after a check, and after a period of searching and critical discussion which generally arises from such a check, than it is in the first instance. Under our system, the power of the cabinet tends to grow at the expense of the House of Commons. The Senate is not so much a check on the House of Commons as it is upon the cabinet, and its influence in this respect undoubtedly is salutary.
I am sure were Sir Clifford Sifton alive today to see the dangerous proportions that the concentration of power in the hands of the cabinet has reached, he would be doubly emphatic upon the necessity for having an impartial, non-partisan, mature, active and vigorous second chamber to keep the ambitions of the executive under control.
Of course, from the standpoint of practical politics a very simple solution would resolve the major difficulty that confronts us in the second chamber at the present time, that is the trend toward domination by one party. A change of administration in the House of Commons would resolve this problem very easily indeed, as it would resolve most other problems that are facing the people of Canada today. Unfortunately, because of the trend toward the one-party state, because of the apathetic condition of the electorate, we have had one party continuously in office for 20 years. The situation has not been resolved on the level of practical politics.
As a result, Mr. Speaker, in the second chamber we see this trend toward one-party domination almost carried to its absolute limit. There are just seven opposition members surviving in the upper chamber today. Such an unhappy state of affairs can only lead to abuse, to a decline in the prestige of this very important arm of our parliamentary

system. The tragedy of it is that today the Senate, which should be a parliamentary institution held in the highest respect by the people of Canada, has tended to become a laughing matter amongst our people. I have been at public meetings, for example, when just a casual reference to the Senate, followed by a pause, brought loud chortles and guffaws from the assembled electorate; and that is a tragic state of affairs when we have the prestige of an integral part of our parliamentary system descending to the level of a joke and a laughing matter.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I interrupt the hon. member to remind him again that to say of the upper house that it is a laughing matter and a tragic joke is not perhaps the sort of courteous remarks this house should be making about the other house which, as he said, is an integral part of parliament. I was just going through some of my notes, and I find that in 1887 the matter of Senate reform was being discussed. I see that at one moment Mr. Charlton, as reported at page 200 of Hansard for April 29, had said this:
The people of Canada recognize it as a useless appendage to the parliament of this country, a packed body of partisans-
At this moment a point of order was raised and the Speaker ruled in this fashion:
The question is now whether two new members ought to be added to the Senate and, of course, it is competent for hon. gentlemen to discuss the advisability of such a measure, and even to dispute the usefulness of that honourable body. As to the expressions used by the honourable member for Both well, I consider them rather objectionable, and I do not think such language ought to be used towards a legislative body which forms a part of our parliament and which, as such, ought to deserve the respect of this house.
I am inclined to adhere to the views expressed on that occasion by Mr. Speaker Ouimet. Hon. members may discuss Senate reform, but I do not think they have to indulge in all kinds of expressions which, if they do think the Senate does not enjoy the prestige it should have, would tend to further lower the prestige of that body.
As I say, under our standing order No. 41, and our practice, we do not allow discourteous remarks with respect to the upper chamber, any more than we would like the upper chamber to employ discourteous remarks with respect to the House of Commons. I think we can carry on a debate on Senate reform without using such strong expressions with respect to our colleagues.

May I venture to point out that the hon. member for Brandon-Souris was not expressing those views himself. He was

quoting the views of other people with regret, and he was not expressing those views himself, as I understood him.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member expressed those views as I heard them. He went further to fortify his stand and said that what he was saying was so much a fact that when he used to attend public meetings and mentioned the Senate, he heard laughs in the assembly. His own opinion as he expressed it, coupled with his reported impression of public meetings he has attended and the way those meetings reacted, prompted me to make the remarks I have made and which I believe are quite justified.

Thank you for those comments, Mr. Speaker. Just before I call it ten o'clock, I think Hansard will indicate that I have expressed the highest admiration for the Senate as an integral and important part of our parliamentary system. That is the whole point of my discussion, that it is a vital
